3rdPartyAuthentication.field.filteringRu:
### Filter Rule

By default, the filter is disabled. You can set a filter rule to filter user information during synchronization.

1. The input syntax of a filter rule is consistent with that of the AD/LDAP filter rule. For more information, see Microsoft Documentations.

- Single rule: (name=filterName)
- Combination rule: (&(name=filterName)(description=departure))(description=departure))

- You can specify an allowlist rule or blocklist rule with the "!" symbol. For allowlist, only the user information configured in the filter rule can be synchronized to the platform. For a blocklist, the user information configured in the filter rule will not be synchronized to the platform.

2. The filter rule length is subject to the AD/LDAP server configurations. Make sure the user-defined length falls within the length.

3. If this parameter is left unconfigured, the system will add a (objectClass=person) rule by default.
3rdPartyAuthentication.field.ldap.sync.m:
### User Mapping

The rule used to map SSO attributes of an SSO user to Cloud attributes. Through the mapping rule, the SSO user has local user attributes after it is synced to the Cloud. For example, if the SSO attribute "cn" of an SSO user is mapped to "User Name", then the User Name of the user is the value of the cn attribute, for example, Bob.
3rdPartyAuthentication.field.mappingOrga:
### Organization Mapping

1.  Subtrees of an organization tree are distinguished by Group parameters, and AD groups will be synchronized to the organizational list in the Cloud (Recommended).
2.  Subtrees of an organization structure tree can be distinguished by OU parameters, and AD groups will be synchronized to the organizational list in the Cloud.
3rdPartyAuthentication.field.mechanism.f:
Filter Mechanism

1. The filtering mechanisms of blocklist and allowlist are both supported.

2. If you select Blocklist, when synchronizing user information, the user information configured in the filter rule will not be synchronized to the Cloud.

3. If you select Allowlist, when synchronizing user information, only the user information configured in the filter rule can be synchronized to the Cloud.

3rdPartyAuthentication.field.sso.sync.ma:
### User Group

Optional. Specify a rule to map the user group of the SSO server to the user group of the Cloud.

1. For example: If a User Group maps usergroup, the User Group created in the Cloud can use the value (such as group-1, group-2) matching usergroup.
2. Note that if the Cloud has multiple user groups that share the same name as the mapped user group, the third-party user will directly join the existing user groups after logging in to the Cloud. If you do not want the synced user to be added to multiple user groups, you can edit the user group name or delete unnecessary user groups.

### User Mapping

The rule used to map SSO attributes of an SSO user to local attributes. Through the mapping rule, the SSO user has local user attributes after it is synced to the platform. For example, if the SSO attribute "cn" of an SSO user is mapped to "User Name", then the User Name of the user is the value of the cn attribute, for example, Bob.

aiStore.upload.model.inferenceTemplate.g: Select an inference template. Click to view {guideHyperLink}

An inference template is a pre-configured software module designed to simplify the deployment of AI models and enhance inference efficiency. Using an inference template, you can quickly integrate a pre-trained model into your enterprise AI platform and immediately start inference tasks.

### How Inference Template Works

An inference template simplifies the model deployment process by pre-defining an inference framework. Therefore, you do not need to set up environments and write code from scratch each time you deploy the  model.

An inference template defines core components, dependencies, and optimized inference code required by the inference framework, ensuring the inference service can run efficiently and stably. The followings are the key elements defines by an inference template:

- **Model**: Defines the path of the target model files to ensure the system correctly loads and uses the model.
- **Inference Code**: Defines the Python code that the model runs when providing inference services, including environment variables and other necessary parameters.
- **Instance Configurations**: Defines the configurations of the instance that the inference service runs on, including the image (operating system, dependencies, etc.) , CPU, memory, compute power, storage, and network.

This platform provides multiple pre-built inference templates for direct use. Additionally, you can configure custom inference templates to meet specific business needs.

### Use and Manage Inference Template

An inference template supports the following actions:

- Used for Model Deployment
  - Used as default inference template: You can attach an inference template to specified models as the default template. When you deploy inference services based on these models, the system uses this template for the deployment by default.
  - Used manually: You can select an inference template (other than the default inference template) when you deploy an inference service based on a model and use this specified template for the deployment.
- Lifecycle Management: You can make full lifecycle management on custom inference templates, including adding, editing, and deleting templates.
- Permission Management: You can set usage permissions of custom inference templates and share them to specified projects/accounts, thus achieving multi-tenant resource isolation.
- Filtering by Inference Framework: You can mark inference templates with their inference frameworks and filter them by the framework type to make categorization management. The following frameworks are supported: 
  - vLLM
  - Diffusers
  - Transformers
  - Sentence Transformers
  - Ollama
  - llama.cpp
  - Others

### Inference Template Compatibility

Different inference templates are designed for different models. Before use, carefully review the definitions and compatibility of the inference templates. Below is a list of pre-built inference templates and their compatible models. You can import these models to the platform and deploy them using the corresponding inference templates.

#### vLLM 0.7.2

vLLM（Virtual Large Language Model）is an inference template specially designed for large language models. It optimizes the memory management and the usage of compute resources, enabling the models to achieve a higher efficient when processing natural languages. The vLLM template is ideal for scenarios requiring high performance and low latency, such as real-time text analysis and intelligent customer service systems.

vLLM 0.7.2 supports the following models. For the model using methods, notifications, and more information, see https://docs.vllm.ai/en/v0.7.2/models/supported_models.html

##### Multimodal Language Models

The following modalities are supported depending on the model:

- **T**ext
- **I**mage
- **V**ideo
- **A**udio

The following lists the meaning of special characters you may find in the tables below: 

- +: This model supports any combination of the listed modalities. For example, T+I means that the model supports text-only, image-only, and text-with-image inputs.
- /: This model supports multiple modalities but these modalities are mutually exclusive. For example, T/I means that the model supports text-only and image-only inputs, but not text-with-image inputs.
- <sup>E</sup>: Pre-computed embeddings can be inputted for this modality.
- <sup>+</sup> : Multiple items can be inputted per text prompt for this modality.

#### Sentence Transformers 3.0.1

The Sentence Transformers inference template focuses on sentence-level semantic similarity computation and text embedding generation. It excels in tasks such as multilingual processing, information retrieval, and recommendation systems. #### llama.cpp-b4739

llama.cpp is an inference framework based on pure C/C++.  It can run pre-trained models in the GGUF format and utilizes the ggml framework at its core. Additionally, it supports CUDA acceleration. Designed for efficient execution of large-scale language models (such as the LLAMA series), llama.cpp supports multiple hardware platforms and significantly reduces model size through quantization techniques while maintaining high inference accuracy.

autoScalingGroup.field.expansion.excuteT:
### Execution Time

If you choose to scale out by month, week, or day, you can configure a more fine-grained scale-out schedule based on your business requirements. For example,

- Scale-out by Month: If you set the execution time to 00:00:00 on the first day of each month, the VM instance is scaled out at 00:00:00 on the first day of each month.
- Scale-out by Week: If you set the execution time to 00:00:00 on Sunday and Tuesday of each week, the VM instance is scaled out at 00:00:00 on Sunday and Tuesday of each week.
- Scale-out by Day: If you set the execution time to 00:30:00, the VM instance is scaled out at 00:30:00 every day.

autoScalingGroup.field.expansionStrategy:
### Scale-out Policy

1. When workloads increase, auto-scaling groups automatically scale out to lower latency and avoid resource restraints.
2. Auto-scaling groups scale out based on the alarm rules that you set for the groups.
3. For example, if the average memory utilization of all VM instances in an auto-scaling group exceeds 80% for a time period, a reasonable number of VM instances are created to accommodate the workloads. This way, the workloads are well balanced at a reasonable level among the VM instances.
autoScalingGroup.field.healthCheckGraceT:
### Health Check Grace Period 
The health check grace period is a period of time after VM instances in the auto-scaling group are created and booted. During this period of time, application services related to these VM instances are probably still booting, and the auto-scaling group will not perform load balancer-based health checks. If this period of time is exceeded, the health status of the VM instances is monitored based on the health check mechanism of the load balancer.
autoScalingGroup.field.healthCheckMethod:
### Health Check Method

The cloud provides the following two health check methods:
1. Load balancer-based health check  

This health check method is a built-in mechanism of load balancers. Load balancers monitor the health status of VM instances in auto-scaling groups. The groups automatically scale out or in based on the health status of the VM instances in the groups. You need to set a health check grace period for this health check method.
 
2. VM health check

This method checks the health status of VM instances in real time. If a VM instance is detected in stopped, unknown, or deleted state, it is considered to be unhealthy.  It is automatically removed from the auto-scaling group and a new VM instance is created. This way, this method ensures that the number of healthy VM instances in an auto-scaling group is not less than the specified minimum number.

### Scale-in Policy

1. When workloads decrease, auto-scaling groups automatically scale in to save resources.
2. Auto-scaling groups scale in based on the alarm rules that you set for the groups.
3. For example, if the average memory utilization of all VM instances in an auto-scaling group keeps lower than 20% for a time period, a reasonable number of VM instances are removed. This way, the workloads are well balanced at a reasonable level among the VM instances.
autoScalingGroup.field.sshPublicKey.tool:
### SSH Public Key

  Inject the SSH public key of a specified VM instance. This allows for password-free logon to the VM instance.
1. Enter the console of the specified VM instance, and run the ssh-keygen command to generate an SSH public key. The key is saved in the ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub file.
2. Before you inject the SSH public key of the VM instance, make sure that cloud-init is installed on the image of the VM instance. We recommend that you install cloud-init 0.7.9, 17.1, 19.4, 19.4, or later.
3. After you install cloud-init, set the ssh_pwauth option in the /etc/cloud/cloud.cfg file to 1. This enables SSH key authentication.
autoScalingGroup.field.userData.tooltip:
### User Data

You can upload user-defined parameters or scripts to customize configurations for VM instances or to accomplish specific tasks.
1. Before you upload user data, make sure that the User Data network service and DHCP service function as expected.
2. Before you upload user data to Linux-based VM instances, make sure that cloud-init is installed on the images of the VM instances. We recommend that you install cloud-init 0.7.9, 17.1, 19.4, 19.4, or later.
3. Before you upload user data to Windows-based VM instances, make sure that  Cloudbase-Init is installed on the images of the VM instances. You can install  Cloudbase-Init of any version.
4. If you set a hostname and root user password in user data, do not set the hostname or root user password by using other methods. This avoids conflicts.
5.  If you set a root user password in user data for a VM instance, the password is displayed in the User Data option on the details page of the VM instance. Make sure that your password is well protected.
6. The following lists the actions that are triggered by a user data script sample. The script is displayed at the bottom.
    - Use ssh-key to create a user named test.
    - Enter the directory path  /etc/hosts, create a directory named /tmp/temp, and then create a file and write data in the file.
    - Set a hostname, enable the root user and SSH login, and then change the root password.
    - Run the echo ls -l / command. 
```  
     #cloud-config users:
name: test shell: /bin/bash groups: users sudo: ['ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL'] ssh-authorized-keys:
ssh-rsa AAAAB3NzaC1LXCJfjroD1lT root@10-0-0-18 bootcmd:
mkdir /tmp/temp write_files:
path: /tmp/ZStack_config content: | Hello,world! permissions: '0755' fqdn: Perf-test disable_root: false ssh_pwauth: yes chpasswd: list: | root:word expire: False runcmd:
echo ls -l / >/root/list.sh
```

backupJob.field.backupRetentionPolicy.lo:
### Local Retention Policy 

1. Set the retention policy for local backup data. Options: by count and by time (day/week/month).

2. If by count, a minimum of 1 local backup can be reserved.

3. If by time, a minimum of 1 day of local backup can be reserved.

A value of n days indicates that starting from the first backup implementation, the local backup data is reserved for 24 hours * n.

A value of n weeks indicates that starting from the first backup implementation, the local backup data is reserved for 7 days * n.

A value of n months indicates that starting from the first backup implementation, the local backup data is reserved for 30 days * n.

### Local Retention Policy

1. Set the policy how the local backup data is reserved. The data can be reserved by count or by time (day/week/month).

2. If by count, a minimum of 1 local backup can be reserved.

3. If by time, a minimum of 1 day of local backup can be reserved.

4. Note: For data generated beyond the retention policy, only the backup records are deleted, which does not affect the data security.
backupJob.field.backupRetentionPolicy.re:
### Remote Retention Policy

1. Set the retention policy for remote backup data. Options: permanent, by count, and by time (day/week/month).

2. If permanent, the remote backup data will not be cleared automatically.

3. If by count, a minimum of 1 remote backup can be reserved.

4. If by time, a minimum of 1 day of remote backup can be reserved.

A value of n days indicates that starting from the first backup implementation, the remote backup data is reserved for 24 hours * n.

A value of n weeks indicates that starting from the first backup implementation, the remote backup data is reserved for 7 days * n.

A value of n months indicates that starting from the first backup implementation, the remote backup data is reserved for 30 days * n.

### Remote Retention Policy

1. Set the policy how the remote backup data is reserved. The data can be reserved permanently, by count, or by time (day/week/month).

2. If permanently, the remote backup data will not be cleared automatically.

3. If by count, a minimum of 1 remote backup can be reserved.

4. If by time, a minimum of 1 day of remote backup can be reserved.

5. Note: For data generated beyond the retention policy, only the backup records are deleted, which does not affect the data security.

1. If you choose to back up data by month, week, or day, you can configure a more fine-grained incremental backup schedule based on your business requirements. For example,
    - Backup by Month: If you set the execution time to 00:00:00 on the first day of each month, the incremental backup job is executed at 00:00:00 on the first day of each month.

backupStorage.field.blobDownloadConcurre:
### Image Blob Download Concurrency

1. Specify the blob download concurrency when you download an image. Default: 1. Valid values: 1 to 16. Increasing blob download concurrency increases the efficiency of creating virtual machines in certain scenarios.

2. To set a blob download concurrency, take the network bandwidth, storage medium, and CPU cores into consideration. A higher concurrency does not necessarily equal a higher image download speed in some scenarios. We recommend that you set the concurrency to 2 if you use a gigabit network and 4-8 if you use a 10-gigabit network.
backupStorage.field.blobUploadConcurrenc:
### Image Blob Upload Concurrency

1. Specify the blob upload concurrency when you upload an image. Default: 1. Valid values: 1 to 16. Increasing blob download concurrency increases the efficiency of cloning virtual machines and creating images.

2. To set a blob upload concurrency, take the network bandwidth, storage medium, and CPU cores into consideration. A higher concurrency does not necessarily equal a higher image upload speed in some scenarios. We recommend that you set the concurrency to 2 if you use a gigabit network and 4-8 if you use a 10-gigabit network. If you use a tape library as the image storage medium, we recommend that you set the concurrency as 1.

When elastic baremetal instances are stopped, baremetal nodes will be automatically released and then can be used by other elastic baremetal instances to avoid idle resources.

1. By performing this operation, baremetal nodes can be modified. At the same time, NIC configurations associated with the elastic baremetal instances will be cleaned up. Hence, if your resources are sufficient, it is recommended not to perform this operation.

bareMetalNode.detail.field.startSource.t:
### Startup Method

The startup method of the baremetal node. The following two startup methods are supported:

#### Volume

Uses a volume as the system volume of the baremetal node to install and deploy the operating system.

#### Local Disk

1. Uses a local disk as the system disk of the baremetal node to install and deploy the operating system.

2. The Local Disk (Non Take-Over) and Local Disk (Take-Over) methods are supported.

- Local Disk (Non Take-Over): When you use the baremetal node to create an elastic baremetal instance, the operating system is downloaded from the Cloud and installed on the elastic baremetal instance. This method will format the local system disk.
- Local Disk (Take-Over): When you use the baremetal node to create an elastic baremetal instance, the original operating system on the local system disk is used as the operating system of the elastic baremetal instance.

bareMetalNode.field.createStyle.tooltip:
### Add Baremetal Node
You can add baremetal nodes manually or by importing a template. You can add a maximum of 500 baremetal nodes to the platform in a batch.

#### Manual Addition
You can specify individual IPMI addresses or an IPMI range to add baremetal nodes.

#### Import Template
1. Download the CSV-formatted template file, enter the information of baremetal nodes in the specified format, and then upload the file. This way, you can add baremetal nodes to the platform.
2. The following describes the syntax of the template:
- The parameters marked with an asterisk  are required. If you do not specify the IMPI Port parameter, the system sets the value of the IMPI Port parameter to 623.
- Startup Method: The startup method of the baremetal nodes. The following three methods are supported:  
   * Remote: Uses a volume as the system volume of the baremetal node to install and deploy the operating system.   
   * Local: Uses a local disk as the system volume of the baremetal node. When you use the baremetal node to create an elastic baremetal instance, the operating system is downloaded from the Cloud and installed on the elastic baremetal instance.
   * Direct: Uses a local disk as the system volume of the baremetal node. When you use the baremetal node to create an elastic baremetal instance, the original operating system on the local system disk is used as the operating system of the elastic baremetal instance.
- Platform Type: The type of platform that you must specify when you specify local for Startup Method. Note that you need to specify the platform type based on the original operating system that you take over. Two types of platforms are supported: Linux and Windows. If you do not specify the platform type, the system specifies Linux for you.
- Reboot to Obtain Hardware Information: Optional. If you enter NO, No, no, N, n, or do not specify the parameter, the baremetal nodes are not rebooted upon creation. If you enter YES, Yes, yes, Y, or y, the baremetal nodes are rebooted upon creation.  
    * If you choose to reboot the baremetal nodes, the hardware information of the baremetal nodes is auto-obtained. This ensures that the baremetal nodes operate as expected and can be used to create elastic baremetal instances.  
    * If you choose to reboot the baremetal nodes, after you add the baremetal nodes to the Cloud, the services on the baremetal nodes are temporarily interrupted.  
    * If you changed the hardware devices of a baremetal node, make sure that the hardware information of the baremetal node that you obtain is the latest.

1. To ensure the baremetal node runs properly and can be used to create an elastic baremetal instance, you need to obtain its hardware information.
2. Obtaining hardware information makes the baremetal node reboot and temporarily interrupts services running on it. To reduce the business impact, you can select business off-peak hours to obtain hardware information after you add the node to the Cloud.
3. If you have obtained the hardware information but hardware changes occur, you need to re-execute the Obtain Hardware Information action to refresh the records on the Cloud.

You can choose whether to take over the original operating system.

- By default, the Take Over Original System is disabled, indicating the Local Disk (Non Take-Over) method is used. When you use the baremetal node to create an elastic baremetal instance, the operating system is downloaded from the Cloud and installed on the elastic baremetal instance.
- If enabled, the Local Disk (Take-Over) method is used. When you use the baremetal node to create an elastic baremetal instance, the original operating system on the local system disk is used as the operating system of the elastic baremetal instance.

barematlInstance.field.networkConfigType:
### Network Configuration

Two types of configurations are supported:
- Identical Configurations: Configures the identical business network topology when baremetal instances are created in bulk.
- Separate Configurations:  Configures corresponding business network topologies for baremetal instances one by one.

#### Notice  
1. To configure business networks, ensure that baremetal instances must have available NICs.
2. If Identical Configurations is used, the NIC count and NIC names of baremetal instances must be identical.
3. You can choose public networks or flat networks. VLAN layer 2 isolation is supported.
4. Ensure that you attach the corresponding L2 network to the baremetal cluster where baremetal chassis reside in advance.
5. If Separate Configurations is used, assign IP addresses for each baremetal instances.

barematlInstance.field.preconfigurationT:
### Bare Metal Template

Select a bare metal template to quickly generate pre-configured files for unattended batch OS installation on bare metal instances.

1. Prepare the bare metal template in advance. Supported types:
    - System template: Provided by default. Contains basic system variables. Ideal for simple unattended deployments.
    - Custom template: Supports user-loaded templates (UTF-8 encoded). Includes basic system variables and customized variables. Ideal for complex unattended deployments.
2. The selected template's operating system must match the selected image.
barematlInstance.field.username.and.pass:
### Set Username and Password
Two types of configurations are supported:
-  Identical Configurations: Centrally configures the identical username and password when baremetal instances are created in bulk.
- Separate Configurations: Configures usernames and passwords for each baremetal instance.
  
#### Notice
  
1. If your operating systems are RHEL/CentOS series and SUSE/openSUSE series, specify only your password since the username defaults to root.
2. If your operating systems are Debian/Ubuntu series, customize your username and password.

baremetal2ChassisOffering.detail.field.s:
### Startup Method

The startup method of the elastic baremetal instance created from an elastic baremetal offering. The following two startup methods are supported:

#### Volume

Uses a volume as the system volume of the elastic baremetal instance created from an elastic baremetal offering to install and deploy the operating system.

#### Local Disk

1. Uses a local disk as the system disk of the elastic baremetal instance created from an elastic baremetal offering to install and deploy the operating system.

2. The Local Disk (Non Take-Over) and Local Disk (Take-Over) methods are supported.

- Local Disk (Non Take-Over): When you create an elastic baremetal instance, the operating system is downloaded from the Cloud and installed on the elastic baremetal instance. This method will format the local system disk.
- Local Disk (Take-Over): When you create an elastic baremetal instance, the original operating system on the local system disk is used as the operating system of the elastic baremetal instance.

baremetalChassis.field.createStyle.toolt:
### Add Mode

1. Two addition methods are supported: manual addition and template import. A maximum of 500 baremetal chassis can be added in bulk at a time.
2. Manual Addition: Assign an IPMI address at a time to add baremetal chassis one by one, or assign an IPMI range to add baremetal chassis in bulk.
3. Template Import: Download the configuration template file in CSV format first, and then upload the file after you complete baremetal chassis configurations according to the stipulated syntax. Finally, perform grammar checks for the file. Notice the following file syntax:
    - The configuration template includes a header and a row of examples. You need to delete or overwrite the example row when you edit the template.
    - Asterisk options are mandatory.  
    - IPMI Address can be used to assign an IPMI address at a time to add baremetal chassis one by one, or assign an IPMI range to add baremetal chassis in bulk. If you enter multiple IPMI ranges, use commas(,) to separate them. You can use "^" to exclude a range, for example, 127.0.0.1-127.0.0.10,^127.0.0.2-127.0.0.3.
    - Set Reboot Baremetal Chassis to optional. If you enter NO/No/no/N/n or leave blank, you need to reboot the baremetal chassis manually to obtain its hardware information. If you enter YES/Yes/yes/Y/y, the baremetal chassis will reboot automatically and you can directly obtain its hardware information.
baremetalChassis.field.name.tooltip:

2. Baremetal chassis must be configured with remote controller cards. Configure IPMI addresses, ports, usernames, and passwords for the remote controller cards, and connect these cards to IPMI networks.
3. PXE boot NICs of baremetal chassis must connect to deployment networks.
4. Other NICs of baremetal chassis must connect to the corresponding L2 network.

bond.field.HashPolicy.tooltip:
### Hash Policy
A bond of LACP mode determines its network export based on a hash computation. Three hash policies are supported: layer2+3, layer 3+4, and layer2.

1. layer2+3: Picks out a NIC port to send data packets based on the hash computation on the source MAC address, destination MAC address, and IP address.
2. layer3+4: Picks out a NIC port to send data packets based on the hash computation on the IP address and port. TCP/IP stacks are supported.
3. layer2: Picks out a NIC port to send data packets based on the hash computation on the source MAC address and destination MAC address.
bond.field.bond.mode.tooltip:
### Bond Mode  
Supports 2 Bond modes: Active-backup (mode1) and LACP (mode4).
1. Active-backup: This mode allows you to bind 1-2 physical NIC ports and we recommend that you bind 2 ports, one acting as the primary port and the other as the secondary port. The primary port handle all network flows by default. When the primary port fails, the secondary port automatically replaces the primary port to handle flows and avoid business interruptions.
2. LACP:
   - Link aggregation control protocol (LACP) mode. This mode allows you to bind 1-8 physical NIC ports and we recommend that you bind at least 2 ports. Bound ports share the same speed and duplex setting. Network flows are evenly sent to the bound ports, thus realizing a load balance.
   - A bond of this mode determines its network export based on a hash computation. Three hash policies are supported: layer2+3, layer 3+4, and layer2.  
     - layer2+3: Picks out a port to send data packets based on the hash computation on the source MAC address, destination MAC address, and IP address.  
     - layer3+4: Picks out a port to send data packets based on the hash computation on the IP address and port. TCP/IP stacks are supported.  
     - layer2: Picks out a port to send data packets based on the hash computation on the source MAC address and destination MAC address.

### Physical NIC Port
1. Add physical NIC ports to the bond. A bond of Active-Backup mode supports 1-2 ports. A bond of LACP mode supports 1-8 ports.
2. We recommend that you add only physical NIC ports of the same type to a bond.
3. Make sure that all NIC ports in a bond have the same speed rate.
4. If you are configuring bonds for more than one host in bulk, a NIC port you select must exist on each of the hosts. For example, to add NIC port eth0 to bonds, make sure that each of the hosts has a NIC port named eth0.

cdpTask.field.cdpRetentionTimePerDay.too:
### Recovery Point Retention Policy

You can set the retention time and retention interval for recovery points. Up to 3 policies can be set.

1. Retention time: You can set how long the recovery points are retained. Valid values: 1–30, integer.

2. Retention interval: You can retain all the recovery points generated in the specified time or retain the recovery points by hour or by day.

      - If by hour, only the recovery points generated at the sharp time are retained.
      - If by day, only the recovery points generated at 00:00 are retained.
      - Retaining recovery points by hour or by day will decrease the number of recovery points, which will save the backup space. We recommend that you choose the retention interval based on your actual needs.

cephStoragePool.tooltip:
### Storage Pool
A storage pool is a logical partition of  Distributed Storage  storages. You can specify a storage pool when you add a  Distributed Storage  storage to the Cloud. If not specified, the Cloud automatically creates a root disk pool, a data disk pool, and an image cache pool.

Note:
1. Before you can specify a storage pool, create one in the corresponding Distributed Storage cluster first.

cluster.field.checkCpuModel.tooltip:
### Host CPU Model Checking Policy

1. Default: Use global setting. That is, the host CPU model is determined by the value of "Host CPU Model Inspection" in the global settings. Values of "Host CPU Model Inspection":
    
 a. true: Indicates that when you hot migrate VM instances or add hosts, the system will check whether the CPU model of the source host is consistent with that of the destination host. If no, you could not hot migrate the VM instances or add the hosts.

 b. false: Indicates that when you hot migrate VM instances or add hosts, the system will not check whether the CPU model of the source host is consistent with that of the destination host.

2. If you select "Check", when you hot migrate VM instances or add hosts, the system will check whether the CPU model of the source host is consistent with that of the host in the current cluster. If no, you could not hot migrate the VM instances or add the hosts.

3. If you select "Not Check", when you hot migrate VM instances or add hosts, the system will not whether the CPU model of the source host is consistent with that of the host in the current cluster.

4. Technically, the consistency of host CPU models in the same cluster can better ensure the successful migration of VM instances.
cluster.field.cpu.overProvisioning.ratio:
### CPU Overcommit Ratio

Controls the number of virtual CPUs allocated to virtual machines. The calculation formula: Physical CPU Total Threads × CPU Overcommit Ratio = Allocatable Virtual CPUs.
cluster.field.cpuModel.tooltip:
### VM CPU Mode

Specifies whether the VMs in the cluster should use the same CPU models as their host to enable access to host CPU features.

#### Options

1. Use Global Setting: The CPU mode of VMs in the cluster is consistent with the global setting CPU Mode.
2. none: The VM CPU model is simulated via QEMU. The VM can access host CPU features to a small degree. This mode is recommended for VM migrations.
3. host-model: The VM CPU model is similar to or the same as that of the host. The VM can access host CPU features to a relatively large degree. This mode can be used for VM migrations.
4. host-passthrough: The VM CPU model is the same as that of the host. The VMs access all host CPU features. This mode supports nested virtualization and is recommended when you have a high requirement for VM CPU features, but it may disable VM migrations through hosts with different CPU models.
5. Custom: All VMs in the cluster use a specified CPU model.

#### Note

1. An x86 cluster supports all CPU modes mentioned above.
2. An aarch64 cluster supports host-passthrough, host-model, and custom.
3. A mips64el or loongarch64 cluster supports the custom mode only.
4. If you set the CPU mode for a VM individually, this cluster setting does not take effect on this VM.
5. If you modify the CPU model, you need to restart VM instances to make the modification take effect.

cluster.storage.info.tooltip:
### Capacity Info

#### I. Utilization

Displays the total capacity and usage of physical CPU, physical memory, and physical storage in the cluster.

#### II. Allocation Ratio

Displays all physical CPU and memory allocations in the cluster.

1. Allocation Ratio = Allocated : Total Overcommit Capacity
2. Total Overcommit Capacity = Physical Total − Reserved Physical Capacity
3. Total Allocatable = Total Overcommit Capacity × Overcommit Ratio
4. Free to Allocate = Total Allocatable − Allocated

#### III. Distribution

Displays the distribution of CPU and memory after overcommitted in the cluster. For more information, see *Capacity Calculation Rules*.

1. CPU Overcommitted Total = Physical CPU Total × Overcommit Ratio
2. Memory Overcommitted Total = Reserved Memory + Total Allocatable Memory Capacity
cluster.tab.gpuDevice.tooltip:
### pGPU Device

1. The following table lists the available physical GPU (pGPU) devices on the host. These GPU devices can be directly passed through to VM instances.
2. Make sure that Intel VT-d or AMD IOMMU is enabled for the host BIOS, and IOMMU support is enabled for the host kernel.
3. Make sure that the IOMMU status of the hosts in the Cloud is "available".
cluster.tab.physicalNic.tooltip:
### Physical NIC  

1. The following table lists all the physical NICs detected on the hosts in the cluster. After you generate virtual functions (VFs) from the physical NICs based on SR-IOV specifications, you can attach the VFs to VM instances.
2. Make sure that Intel VT-d/AMD IOMMU and SR-IOV are enabled for the host BIOS in the cluster. 
3. Make sure that the IOMMU status of the hosts in the Cloud is "available".
cluster.tab.usbDevice.tooltip:
### USB Device

1. The following table lists the USB devices of hosts in the cluster. You can directly pass through the USB devices to VM instances.
2. A VM instance can have a maximum of 1 USB 1.x device, 6 USB 2.x devices, and 4 USB 3.x devices attached.
cluster.tab.vGPU.tooltip:
### vGPU Device

1. The following table lists the vGPU devices generated from physical GPU (pGPU) devices on the host. You can attach these vGPU devices to VM instances.
2. Make sure that Intel VT-d or AMD IOMMU is enabled for the host BIOS and IOMMU support is enabled for the host kernel.
3. Make sure that the status of host IOMMU in the Cloud is "available".
4. You can generate VFs from NVIDIA and AMD pGPU devices based on fixed specifications. Note that NVIDIA allows you to generate VFs from each pGPU device on the host, while AMD allows you to generate VFs from all pGPU devices on the host.

## Console UI Proxy Address

This address is used to proxy access to the VM console UI. You can set it to an IP address or a domain name. If left blank, the system uses a default proxy address.

### Bond Mode

Provide 3 physical NIC port bonding modes.

1. Active-Backup: All network traffic is handled by the primary port. If the primary port fails, traffic automatically switches to the backup port to avoid service interruption.
2. Balance-SLB: Distributes network traffic across ports based on source MAC address and VLAN ID to achieve load balancing.
3. Balance-TCP: Distributes network traffic across ports based on TCP flow's source/destination IP addresses and port numbers for more granular load balancing.

create.vswitch.bond.field.bond.mode.tool:
### Bond Mode

1. LACP Mode:

    - Supports bonding 1 to 8 physical ports. Bonding at least 2 ports is recommended. Bonded ports share the same speed and duplex settings. Network traffic is distributed evenly across the ports for load balancing.
    - This mode uses a hash algorithm to determine the egress port for network traffic.
    
2. Active-Backup Mode:

    - Supports bonding 1 to 8 physical ports. Bonding 2 ports is recommended.
    - After bonding, one port acts as the active port, while the others serve as backup ports. All network traffic is handled by the active port. If the active port fails, traffic automatically fails over to a backup port to maintain service continuity.
create.vswitch.bond.field.bond.name.tool:
### Uplink Name

An uplink name represents the bonded physical ports on a host that connect to a physical switch.

1. By default, uplinks are named in the format "Uplink+suffix", where the suffix is an auto-incrementing number (1, 2, 3...) to distinguish resources. If the number of uplinks is 10 or more, the default naming format changes to "Up+suffix".
2. You can specify a custom name. The name must be 1 to 10 characters long and can contain letters, numbers, hyphens (-), or underscores (_). The name cannot start with a number.

customHomepage.modal.welcome.item.descri: Supports adding HUAWEI iMaster NCE-Fabric V100R023 SDN controllers to the Cloud, enabling automated deployment of network configurations and resource isolation on the SDN tenant level.

Reduces hardware costs and improves security resource utilization by virtualizing and passing through the embedded security coprocessor (CCP) to VM instances. Efficiently meets compliance requirements, including classified cybersecurity protection and cryptography assessment.

Enables flexible allocation and high availability of high-performance network resources. Improves network throughput and reduces latency while providing link redundancy and failover capabilities.
Supports seamless integration with mainstream identity providers (IdPs) via the SAML 2.0 protocol, allowing enterprise accounts to log in to the Cloud using single sign-on (SSO).

Enables one-click migration of multiple VM instances to target hosts or primary storage, reducing the complexity of large-scale operations such as planned maintenance, storage expansion, and load rebalancing, while eliminating the risk of business interruption.

Adds support for mainstream GuestOS, including Ubuntu 24, RHEL 10, Windows Server 2025, Rocky Linux 10, and AnolisOS 8. All these GuestOS are compatible with VM GuestTools, enabling enhanced performance and extended functionality.
Enables shared license quotas across multiple platforms, helping enterprises improve asset utilization and operational efficiency in multi-environment collaboration scenarios.

1. You can configure a backup schedule by week, day, hour. Based on the specified backup cycle, you need to set a more fine-grained time for backup, accurate to the minute.

database.backup.strategy.execute.time.to:
### Execution Time

For backup by week or day, you can set a fine-grained execution time for the backup plan, with the support for selection down to the minute level.

- Backup by week: If you set the execution time to 00:00 on Sunday and Tuesday of each week, the backup plan is executed at 00:00:00 on Sunday and Tuesday of each week.
- Backup by day: If you set the execution time to 00:30, the backup plan is executed at 00:30:00 every day.
database.local.backup.retention.policy.t:
### Local Retention Policy

Set the policy how local backup data is retained. The backup data can be retained by quantity or by time (day/week/month).

- By quantity: Retains a minimum of 1 local backup data.
- By time: Retains a minimum of 1 day of local backup data.

Note: For data generated beyond the retention policy, only the backup records are deleted, which does not affect the data security.
database.remote.retention.policy.tooltip:
### Remote Retention Policy

Set the policy how remote backup data is retained. The backup data can be retained permanently, by quantity, or by time (day/week/month).

- Permanently: The remote backup data will not be cleared automatically.
- By quantity: Retains a minimum of 1 remote backup data.
- By time: Retains a minimum of 1 day of remote backup data.

Note: For data generated beyond the retention policy, only the backup records are deleted, which does not affect the data security.

find.bareMetalChassis.description:
### Obtain Hardware Information
1. To ensure the baremetal node runs properly and can be used to create an elastic baremetal instance, you need to obtain its hardware information.
2. Obtaining hardware information may make the baremetal node reboot, temporarily interrupting services running on the node and stopping the elastic baremetal instance on it. To reduce the business impact, you can select business off-peak hours to execute this action.
3. If you want to ensure business continuity and obtain the hardware information without rebooting the baremetal node, satisfy the following requirements:
    - You have created an elastic baremetal instance based on the baremetal node.
    - The elastic baremetal instance in Connected.
    - The elastic baremetal instance uses a Linux operating system.
    - The elastic baremetal instance is installed with an agent of 2.0.8 or later version.
    - If any one of the above requirements is not met, the system will automatically reboot the baremetal node when you obtain its hardware information.
4. If you have obtained the hardware information but hardware changes occur, you need to re-execute the Obtain Hardware Information action to refresh the records on the Cloud.

firewall.field.name.tooltip:
### Firewall

1. A firewall is a layer-3 access control policy that monitors north-south traffic of VPC networks and filters TCP, UDP, ICMP, and other types of data packets that flow in and out of VPC vRouters.
2. You can associate a rule set that has one or more rules with the NICs of a VPC vRouter to monitor traffic that flows in or out of the NICs. This ensures the security of the VPC vRouter and the communication security of the whole VPC network.
3. You can customize the priority of a firewall rule and decide for the rule whether to accept, drop, or reject data.
firewall.glossary: A firewall is an access control policy that monitors incoming and outgoing traffic of VPC vRouters and decides whether to allow or block specific traffic based on a defined set of security rules.
firewall.modal.delete.danger: Deleting a firewall also deletes the rules that are associated with the firewall. Proceed with caution.

flat.network.field.dhcp.service.ip.toolt:
### DHCP IP
1. The DHCP IP address is the IP address occupied by the DHCP service. Based on this IP address, the DHCP service will assign IP addresses to VM instances that mount this L3 network.
2. If you create the L3 network and enable the DHCP service for the first time, or add the first network range for the L3 network that has the DHCP service enabled, you can customize the DHCP IP address.
3. If the DHCP service has already been added to the L3 network, adding a network range will not let you customize the DHCP IP address.
4. The DHCP IP address can be outside or inside the added IP range, but must fall within the CIDR where the added IP address belongs, and this DHCP IP address must not be occupied.
1. Deleting a network range also detaches the VM NICs that are using the network range. Please exercise caution.

2. If the L3 network has a DHCP IP that is in the selected network range, deleting the network range does not delete the DHCP IP. If all network ranges under the L3 network are deleted, the DHCP IP will be released.

flatNetwork.field.name.tooltip:

For backup by month or week, you can set a fine-grained full backup execution time, with the support for selection down to the minute level.

- Backup by month: If you set the execution time to 00:00 on the first day of each month, the full backup is executed at 00:00:00 on the first day of each month.
- Backup by week: If you set the execution time to 00:00 on Sunday and Tuesday of each week, the full backup is executed at 00:00:00 on Sunday and Tuesday of each week.

Timeout for Creating Disk Image from Data Disk

Timeout for Creating Disk Image from Disk 1

Specify the maximum timeout limit for creating a disk image from disk 1. If the creation exceeds this time limit, the operation will fail. Default: 3 days. Unit: second, minute, hour, and day.
Timeout Period of Creating Root Volume Image from Volume Snapshot

globalConfig.applianceVm.agent.deployOnS: Specifies whether to enable auto deployment of agent process when a VPC vRouter is started. Default: false. If set to true, the management node does not check the agent version on the VPC vRouter and directly deploys a new agent each time a VPC vRouter is created, started, or restarted.

globalConfig.applianceVm.ssh.timeout.des: The timeout period that the management node establishes a SSH connection with a VPC vRouter. Default: 300. Unit: second. If the management node fails to establish a SSH connection with a VPC vRouter, the VPC vRouter fails to be started and is deleted.

globalConfig.backupStorage.connection.au: Auto-Reconnection to Image Storage and Local Backup Server

Specifies whether to enable automatic reconnection if a backup storage or local backup server is disconnected. Default: true. This value indicates that the management node auto reconnects a backup storage or local backup server if the server is disconnected.
Maximum Failed Attempt to Reconnect Image Storage and Local Backup Server

The maximum number of failed attempts of the management node to automatically reconnect backup storages or local backup servers. If the number of attempts exceeds the threshold, the management node stops reconnecting the backup storages or local backup servers. Default: 0. globalConfig.baremetalInstance.deletionP:
### Bare Metal Instance Deletion Policy

Specify the deletion policy for bare metal instances. Default: Never Delete. Options include Immediate Deletion and Never Delete.

- Immediate Deletion: The bare metal instance is directly expunged as soon as you delete it.
- Never Delete: 
    - The bare metal instance is moved to the Recycle Bin after deletion and will not be automatically expunged. You can recover a deleted bare metal instance from the Recycle Bin.
    - Bare metal instances in the Recycle Bin can be manually expunged. Once expunged, they cannot be recovered. Proceed with caution.
globalConfig.billing.billing.currency.sy: The currency symbol used for billing. Valid values: ￥, $, €, £, A$, HK$, ¥, CHF, C$, and Rp.
globalConfig.billing.billing.enable.desc: Specifies whether to enable the billing feature. Default: true. If set to false, resources are not billed.
The time when a bill is generated. Default: 0:00.
globalConfig.cdp.concurrent.start.level: CDP task startup and concurrency degree.
Default is 2, unit is individual, ranging from 1 to 16, used to set the maximum number of concurrent CDP tasks supported by backup servers for startup. If the number of concurrently started CDP tasks exceeds the set threshold, excess CDP tasks will be placed in a queue and wait.

globalConfig.ceph.image.expiration.time: Retention Period for Deleted Data in Ceph Primary Storage
Image data deleted from Ceph primary storage will be retained in a recycle bin (Trash) for a period before it is expunged. During this period, you can recover deleted data from the recycle bin. After this period, the data is regarded as expired. Expired data is expunged regularly and cannot be recovered. Default value: 604800. Unit: second (604800s = 7 days). If you set it as 0, the data is not saved in the recycle bin and is expunged directly after the deletion.
globalConfig.ceph.imageCache.cleanup.int: Ceph Distributed Storage Image Cache Cleanup Interval

The interval of cleaning image caches from Ceph distributed storage. This setting is applied after images in distributed storage are deleted and image caches are no longer used by virtual machines. Default: 43,200. Unit: second.

Specifies whether to enable database recovery from backup data when data exists in the database. Default: true.
globalConfig.drs.drs.migrateVm.concurren: The maximum number of VM instances that can be simultaneously migrated from the current host to the destination host while implementing dynamic resource scheduling. Default: 1.

globalConfig.glossary: Global Setting allows you to configure settings that take effect on the whole platform.

If set to true, hosts across clusters can be detected to achieve VM high availability. Before you enable this feature, make sure that clusters are well connected.

### VM HA
1. Specifies whether to enable high availability for virtual machines. Default: true.

2. If set to false, the high availability feature is disabled globally for virtual machines. Please proceed with caution.
globalConfig.ha.host.check.interval.desc:
### Abnormal Host Status Update Interval

The interval for the system to check and update the status of abnormal hosts. Default: 5. Unit: second.
globalConfig.ha.host.check.maxAttempts: Minimum Connection Attempts Required to Determine Host is Disconnected
globalConfig.ha.host.check.maxAttempts.d:
### Minimum Connection Attempts Required to Determine Host is Disconnected

The maximum times for the system to attempt to connect to a host. If the system fails to connect to the host after the specified times of attempt, the host is determined as disconnected. Default: 12.
globalConfig.ha.host.check.successInterv: Ping Response Time to Determine Host Connection is Established Successfully

### Ping Response Time to Determine Host Connection is Established Successfully

The time period for the system to wait the host response after it pings the host. Receiving a response within this period indicates that the system establishes a successful connection with the host. Default: 5. Unit: second.
globalConfig.ha.host.check.successRatio: Minimum Connection Success Rate to Determine Host is Re-Connected
### Minimum Connection Success Rate to Determine Host is Re-Connected

The minimum rate of successful connections occupied in total connection attempts to determine a disconnected host is successfully re-connected. Default: 50. Unit: %.
globalConfig.ha.host.check.successTimes: Minimum Successful Connections Required to Determine Host is Re-Connected
### Minimum Successful Connections Required to Determine Host is Re-Connected

globalConfig.ha.host.selfFencer.interval: The interval that a host inspects its own status. Default: 5. Unit: second.
globalConfig.ha.host.selfFencer.maxAttem: The maximum number of attempts that a host inspects its own status. If the self-inspection of a host fails by the maximum attempts, it is determined that network errors occur with the host. Default: 6.
globalConfig.ha.host.selfFencer.storageC: Timeout Period for Host Connecting to Data Storage

globalConfig.ha.neverStopVm.gc.maxRetryI: Maximum Interval for VM Attempt to HA Start

### Maximum Interval for VM Attempt to HA Start

### VM Retry HA Start Inverval

The interval for a Neverstop VM to retry an HA start after the previous HA start attempt fails. Default: 60. Unit: second.
globalConfig.ha.neverStopVm.scan.interva:
### HA VM State Scanning Interval

The interval to scan the status of a NeverStop VM after it fails to HA start. Default: 60. Unit: second.
### HA VM State Update Speed

The speed of updating the state of NeverStop virtual machines on the UI. Default: 1. Valid values: -1 to 5. A higher value indicates a lower update speed. However, a lower update speed makes the system ignore a lot of outdated notifications, thus decreasing the system workload. If set to -1, the NeverStop VM states on the UI are not updated automatically.
globalConfig.ha.self.fencer.strategy.des:
### High Availability Policy

1. The high availability policy of virtual machines. Default: Permissive. Valid values: Permissive and Force.

2. The value Permissive indicates that if a virtual machine is in unknown state, the management node does not migrate the virtual machine and the self fencer process that runs on the host does not stop the virtual machine.

3. The value Force indicates that if the condition that triggers high availability migration is met, the management node migrates the virtual machine to another host.
globalConfig.ha.vm.ha.level.alert: If you specifically set VM HA mode for a virtual machine, this global setting does not take effect on the virtual machine.
globalConfig.ha.vm.ha.level.description:
### HA Mode
Specifies whether to enable auto restart if virtual machines are scheduled or unexpectedly stopped or are errored because of errors occurring to compute, network, or storage resources associated with the virtual machines.  Valid values: None and NeverStop.

1. If you set HA mode to None, virtual machines scheduled or unexpectedly stopped are not auto restarted.

2. If you set HA mode to NeverStop:

- virtual machines scheduled or unexpectedly stopped are auto restarted.
- If errors occur to compute, network, or storage resources, associated virtual machines are auto restarted on another host depending on the HA policy you configure for them.

Note that you can specifically set VM HA mode for a virtual machine. If you do, this System Parameter does not take effect on the virtual machine.
globalConfig.host.connection.autoReconne: Auto Reconnect Host on Ping Failure

### Auto Reconnect Host on Ping Failure

Specify whether to automatically reconnect hosts to the management node, if the management node fails to ping hosts. Default: enabled.

### Host Max Reconnection Failures

Specify the maximum number of consecutive failed reconnection attempts allowed by the management node before it stops trying to reconnect to a host. Default: 0.
globalConfig.host.cpu.overProvisioning.r:
1. An excessively large value may greatly reduce host performance and cause application stuck.

globalConfig.kvm.vm.cpuMode.description:
### Virtual Machine CPU Mode

This setting allows you to configure whether virtual machines inherit the CPU model and features of their host machine or emulate a different CPU type. This can be useful for meeting specific business requirements.

Optional modes:

1. None (default): The platform emulates a CPU type, which is a subset of the host machine's CPU features.
2. Compatible: The virtual machine's CPU model is set to match the host machine's CPU model as closely as possible. This mode is recommended for migration scenarios.
3. Passthrough: The virtual machine's CPU model and features are identical to those of the host machine. This mode provides the most accurate CPU emulation, but may cause issues with nested virtualization or migration between different CPU types.
4. Custom (specific CPU model): The virtual machine is configured to emulate a specific CPU type. This mode allows you to specify a custom CPU model that is different from the host machine's CPU.

Notes:

1. Passthrough mode supports nested virtualization, but may cause issues with migration between different CPU types or viewing CPU usage rates.
2. This System Parameter only applies to x86_64 CPU architectures.
3. If a virtual machine has already been configured with a custom CPU model, this System Parameter will not take effect for that virtual machine.
4. If a cluster has been configured to specify a virtual machine's CPU model, this System Parameter will not take effect for that cluster.
5. After modifying the CPU mode, you must restart the virtual machine for the changes to take effect.

### Host Allocation Strategy

1. Specify the host allocation strategy to be used when creating new virtual machines. Default: Host with min. running VMs.

     - Host with min. CPU utilization: The host with the minimum CPU utilization will be chosen to create virtual machines.
    - Host with min. memory utilization: The host with the minimum memory utilization will be chosen to create virtual machines.
    - Host with max. running VMs: The host with the maximum number of running virtual machines will be chosen to create virtual machines. To use this option, you need to set the maximum number of virtual machines that can run on a host. Then, the system chooses the host that meets the requirements to create virtual machines. If no host is available, you would fail to create a virtual machine.
    - Host where the VM located last time: When you restart a stopped virtual machine, the system chooses the host where the VM was running last time. If you start a new virtual machine for the first time, the system chooses a host randomly.
    - Random allocation: The system randomly chooses a host to create virtual machines.

2. If you choose the "Host with min. CPU utilization" or "Host with min. memory utilization" strategy, you can set the interval for collecting the CPU utilization and memory utilization in the system parameters.

SAN Storage  Storage Distribution Policy

1. The policy used to distribute a SAN Storage LUN to a disk and snapshot. Valid values: none (default), minLvCounts, and maxFreeSize.
2. If you select none, when you create a disk or snapshot, a  SAN Storage  LUN that has sufficient spaceis is distributed to the disk or snapshot based on the system scheduling.
3. If you select minLvCounts, when you create a disk or snapshot, the  SAN Storage  LUN that has the smallest total number of disks and snapshots and has sufficient available space is distributed to the disk or snapshot.
4. If you select maxFreeSize, when you create a disk or snapshot, the  SAN Storage  LUN that has the the most available space is distributed to the disk or snapshot.

Specify the control policy of multipath access to data storage.

- Disable: Disable the multipath service of the platform. If disabled, only single path access is supported.

### Virtual Machine Cache Mode
Default value is none, used to set virtual machine cache mode. Optional modes include: writethrough, none, writeback.

* none:
    - The virtual machine does not use host page cache and accesses the host hard disk directly.
    - Suitable for scenarios where data real-time synchronization is required.
    
* writethrough:
    - Data is written to host page cache first, then written to host hard disk.
    - Suitable for scenarios where high data consistency requirements are needed.
    
* writeback:
    - Data is written to host page cache first, and synchronized with host hard disk when the cache area is full or a write-back operation is triggered.
    - Suitable for scenarios where high write performance is required.

### Virtual Machine CPU Mode

This setting allows you to configure whether virtual machines inherit the CPU model and features of their host machine or emulate a different CPU type. This can be useful for meeting specific business requirements.

Optional modes:

1. None (default): The platform emulates a CPU type, which is a subset of the host machine's CPU features.
2. Compatible: The virtual machine's CPU model is set to match the host machine's CPU model as closely as possible. This mode is recommended for migration scenarios.
3. Passthrough: The virtual machine's CPU model and features are identical to those of the host machine. This mode provides the most accurate CPU emulation, but may cause issues with nested virtualization or migration between different CPU types.
4. Custom (specific CPU model): The virtual machine is configured to emulate a specific CPU type. This mode allows you to specify a custom CPU model that is different from the host machine's CPU.

Notes:

1. Passthrough mode supports nested virtualization, but may cause issues with migration between different CPU types or viewing CPU usage rates.
2. This System Parameter only applies to x86_64 CPU architectures.
3. If a virtual machine has already been configured with a custom CPU model, this System Parameter will not take effect for that virtual machine.
4. If a cluster has been configured to specify a virtual machine's CPU model, this System Parameter will not take effect for that cluster.
5. After modifying the CPU mode, you must restart the virtual machine for the changes to take effect.

### VM Deletion Policy

Specify whether to completely delete the virtual machine or retain it in the recycle bin when you delete a virtual machine. Default: Delayed Deletion. Options include Immediate Deletion, Delayed Deletion, and Never Delete.

1. Immediate Deletion:
    - The virtual machine is directly expunged as soon as you delete it. An expunged VM cannot be recovered. Proceed with caution.
    - Any virtual machines currently in the Recycle Bin will also be expunged as soon as you apply this policy. Proceed with caution.

2. Delayed Deletion:
    - The virtual machine is moved to the Recycle Bin after deletion. You can specify a retention period during which the virtual machine is retained in Recycle Bin. After the retention period expires, the virtual machine is automatically expunged and cannot be recovered.
    - You can recover a deleted virtual machine from the Recycle Bin before it is automatically expunged.

3. Never Delete:
    - The virtual machine is moved to the Recycle Bin after deletion and will not be automatically expunged. You can recover a deleted virtual machine from the Recycle Bin.
    - Virtual machines in the Recycle Bin can be manually expunged. Once expunged, they cannot be recovered. Proceed with caution.

globalConfig.vm.deletionPolicy.descripti:
### VM Deletion Policy

Specify whether to completely delete the virtual machine or retain it in the recycle bin when you delete a virtual machine. Default: Delayed Deletion. Options include Immediate Deletion, Delayed Deletion, and Never Delete.

1. Immediate Deletion:
    - The virtual machine is directly expunged as soon as you delete it. An expunged VM cannot be recovered. Proceed with caution.
    - Any virtual machines currently in the Recycle Bin will also be expunged as soon as you apply this policy. Proceed with caution.

2. Delayed Deletion:
    - The virtual machine is moved to the Recycle Bin after deletion. You can specify a retention period during which the virtual machine is retained in Recycle Bin. After the retention period expires, the virtual machine is automatically expunged and cannot be recovered.
    - You can recover a deleted virtual machine from the Recycle Bin before it is automatically expunged.

3. Never Delete:
    - The virtual machine is moved to the Recycle Bin after deletion and will not be automatically expunged. You can recover a deleted virtual machine from the Recycle Bin.
    - Virtual machines in the Recycle Bin can be manually expunged. Once expunged, they cannot be recovered. Proceed with caution.

### Recycle Bin Expired Resources Cleanup Interval

Specify the time interval for automatic cleanup of expired resources in the recycle bin. Default: 1 hour. Unit: hour. The interval can be set as an integer between 1 and 24. When resources under the delayed deletion policy reach their preset retention time in the recycle bin, the system will check for expired resources at the specified interval and automatically clean them up.
globalConfig.vm.expungePeriod.descriptio:
Defaulting to \"Delete after delay\"", used for setting the deletion strategy for cloud hosts and elastic bare metal instances. Optional strategies include: Delete immediately, Delete after delay, Never delete.

Delete immediately: When a user deletes a cloud host or an elastic bare metal instance, these cloud hosts or elastic bare metal instances will be deleted immediately.

Delete after delay: When a user deletes a cloud host or an elastic bare metal instance, these cloud hosts or elastic bare metal instances will be marked as deleted and displayed in the corresponding \"Deleted\" tab. They will only be permanently deleted after the default delay period (defaulting to 9 days) has elapsed or when the user forces deletion manually.

Never delete: When a user deletes a cloud host or an elastic bare metal instance, these cloud hosts or elastic bare metal instances will never be automatically deleted by the system.

globalConfig.vm.spiceStreamingMode.descr: Default: off. Valid values: off, all, and filter. The value all indicates that all video frames are encoded, compressed, and then transferred. This lowers bandwidth requirements, promotes streaming fluency, while increases the CPU pressure of thin clients. The value filter indicates that incremental video frames are encoded, compressed, and then transferred. Compared with the all mode, this mode further lowers bandwidth requirements and promotes streaming fluency. The CPU pressure of thin clients is relatively low. However, Chrome flash of thin clients will cause streaking issues. The value off indicates that video frames are not encoded or compressed before transmission. This produces HD video streaming while have highest requirements for bandwidth. The CPU pressure of thin clients is the lowest among the three modes.

### GPU Policy

1. Attach pGPUs or vGPUs to the VM instance.

   - pGPU: Passthrough a physical GPU device to the VM instance.
   - vGPU: Attach a vGPU device which is virtually divided from a pGPU to the VM instance.

2. Supports two GPU attachment policies:

   - Attach GPU Device: Select a GPU device and attach it directly to the VM instance.
   - Attach GPU Specification: Select a GPU specification and the system allocates GPU device(s) to the VM instance according to this specification. You can choose whether to make these GPU device(s) automatically detached when the VM is stopped.
      - Auto Detach: When the VM is stopped, these GPU device(s) are automatically detached. When the VM starts, the system re-allocates GPU device(s) to it according to the GPU specification.
      - Do not Auto Detach: When the VM is stopped, it keeps these GPU device(s) attached. However, if the VM is stopped unexpectedly, it cannot automatically start even though its HA mode is NeverStop.

### IPv4 Address

1. If you are configuring bonds in bulk, the system assigns IPv4 addresses successively in the address range based on the start IPv4 and netmask. The broadcast and network addresses are skipped automatically. For example, if you are configuring 3 bonds with the start IPv4 as 192.168.20.254 and netmask as 255.255.255.0, the system assigns 192.168.20.254, 192.168.21.1, and 192.168.21.2 to these 3 bonds respectively.

host.field.createStyle.cube.tooltip:
### Add Host
You can add hosts by using either of the following methods: scan-based addition, manual addition, and template import. manually or by importing a template. You can add a maximum of 500 hosts to the platform in a batch by using manual addition and template import methods. Scan-based addition has no such limit.
#### Manual Addition
You can specify individual IP addresses or an IP range to add hosts.
#### Scan-based Addition
Available hosts are auto discovered. You can scan the hosts and then add them to the Cloud as hyper-converged nodes or compute nodes
#### Import Template
1. Download the CSV-formatted template file, enter the information of hosts in the specified format, and then upload the file. This way, you can add hosts to the platform.
2. The following describes the syntax of the template:

    - The parameters marked with an asterisk (*) are required. If you do not specify the Name or SSH Port parameter, the system sets the value of the Name parameter in the fomat of HOST-host IP address and the value of the SSH Port parameter to 22.

    - You can specify individual IP addresses or IP ranges for the Host IP parameter. If you specify multiple IP addresses, separate each IP range with a comma (,). Caret (^) indicates exclusion, for example, 127.0.0.1-127.0.0.10,^127.0.0.2-127.0.0.3.

    - The Scan Host IOMMU Setting parameter is optional. If you set the parameter to NO, No, no, N, or n, or left the parameter blank, the host IOMMU setting scanning feature is disabled.  If you set the parameter to YES, Yes, yes, Y, or y, the host IOMMU setting scanning feature is enabled.

    - The Disable Intel EPT Hardware Assist parameter is optional. If you set the parameter to NO, No, no, N, or n, or left the parameter blank, the Intel EPT hardware assist feature is enabled.  If you set the parameter to YES, Yes, yes, Y, or y, the Intel EPT hardware assist feature is disabled.

3. You can add only KVM-based hosts in the template.

host.storage.info.tooltip:
### Capacity Info

#### I. Utilization

Displays the total capacity and usage of physical CPU, physical memory, and physical storage in the host.

#### II. Allocation Ratio

Displays the CPU, memory, and storage allocations in the host.

1. Allocation Ratio = Allocated : Total Overcommit Capacity
2. Total Overcommit Capacity = Physical Total − Reserved Physical Capacity
3. Total Allocatable = Total Overcommit Capacity × Overcommit Ratio
4. Free to Allocate = Total Allocatable − Allocated

#### III. Distribution

Displays the distribution of CPU, memory, and storage after overcommitted in the host. For more information, see *Capacity Calculation Rules*.

1. CPU Overcommitted Total = Physical CPU Total × Overcommit Ratio
2. Memory Overcommitted Total = Reserved Memory + Total Allocatable Memory Capacity
3. Storage Overcommitted Total = Reserved Capacity + Total Allocatable Storage Capacity

image.action.storage.migration.tooltip:
### Change Image Storage

Supports image migrations between distributed image storage.

- To migrate images, make sure the monitoring nodes of the two distributed image storage are interconnected.
- If you migrate an ISO image to an image storage of another data center, the virtual machine using this image cannot be powered on. You need to detach the ISO image from the virtual machine and then you can power on the VM as expected.
- After the migration, the original data of the image will be retained in the image storage. You can manually clean up the data in the image storage. The data cannot be recovered after it is deleted. Proceed with caution.

image.field.architecture.tooltip:
CPU Architecture

1. Select a CPU architecture for the image. VM instances created from the image use this CPU architecture.  
2. If you select aarch64 or mips64, set the BIOS mode to UEFI.
image.field.biosMode.tips: Select the BIOS mode carefully. Mode mismatch may cause VM instances unable to work properly.
image.field.biosMode.tooltip:
### BIOS Mode

When you select a BIOS mode for images of different formats, note that: 
   - For qcow2 and raw images, select the BIOS mode that is consistent with the template. 
   - For iso images, you can select a BIOS mode as needed. Then, the system will be booted accordingly.

The BIOS modes include Legacy and UEFI.
   - Legacy:  Supports x86 architectures and all operating systems.  
   - UEFI: If the CPU architecture is AArch64 or MIPS64EL, you must use UEFI. Supported operating systems include Windows and CentOS. Note if you use Windows 7 or WindowsServer 2008, CSM need to be used.

image.field.compatibility.tooltip:
### Compatibility Support Module

1. The Compatibility Support Module (CSM) is used only to provide compatibility support for operating systems that do not support or cannot fully support UEFI.

2. CSM is used if you use Windows 7/2008. If you select Windows, we recommend you do not select CSM.
image.field.imagePath.tooltip:
### Image Path

#### URL

1. Use the specified URL to add images. 
2. Supported formats:
    - HTTP/HTTPS/FTP/SFTP. Examples:
        - http://host[:port]/path/file
        - https://host[:port]/path/file
        - ftp://[user:password@]hostname[:port]/path/file 
        - sftp://user[:password]@hostname[:port]/path/file  
    - The absolute path on an image storage, which supports standalone image storage. Examples:
        - file:///path/file  
3. Make sure that the URL you entered here can be accessed by the image storage, and the image file is available.   
4. If you use the SFTP format with no password specified, make sure that you can SSH to the specified host without a password. 

#### Local File

1. Upload an image file that can be accessed by your current browser. Note that standalone image storage and distributed image storage are supported.  
2. Select a file that matches the format of the selected image.
image.field.imageType.tooltip:
### Image Type

1. A system image contains an OS for running services. You can use a system image to create VM instances. A system image can be of the ISO or Image type.
2. A volume image contains only service data. You can use a volume image to create volumes. A volume image can only be of the Image type.
3. Image-type images can be in raw, qcow2, and vmdk format.
4. Images are stored on image storage. When an image is used to create a VM instance or volume, the image is downloaded to a primary storage and cached there.

image.field.platform.tooltip:
### Platform

The image platform determines the platform used for creating VM instances. You can set whether to use KVM VirtIO drivers (including disk drivers and NIC drivers).

1. Linux: If VirtIO is enabled, the image operating system (OS) will have a VirtIO driver attached. If VirtIO is disabled, the OS, such as RHEL 5.8, will use a QEMU device instead.

2. Windows: If VirtIO is enabled, the image OS will have a VirtIO driver attached. If VirtIO is disabled, the OS will use a QEMU device instead.

3. Other: If VirtIO is enabled, the image OS will have a VirtIO driver attached. If VirtIO is disabled, the OS will use a QEMU device instead. This type of platform is compatible with some operating systems of earlier versions that do not support VirtIO drivers.
image.field.supporting.elasticBaremetal2:
### Support Elastic Baremetal Instance

Identifies whether the image can be used to create elastic baremetal instances. If this checkbox is selected, the image can be used to create elastic baremetal instances.

1. Make sure that an agent is installed for the image of the elastic baremetal instance. Otherwise, you cannot open the console, change the password of the elastic baremetal instance, or attach/detach volumes and networks.
2. Make sure that the BIOS mode of the image used to create elastic baremetal instances is the same as the system configuration. The default mode is UEFI. If you need to use Legacy, contact our official technical support.
image.field.supportingElasticBaremetal2I:

Identifies whether the image can be used to create elastic baremetal instances. If this checkbox is selected, the image can be used to create elastic baremetal instances.

2. Make sure that the BIOS mode of the image used to create elastic baremetal instances is the same as the system configuration. The default mode is UEFI. If you need to use Legacy, contact our official technical support.

incremental.backup.strategy.execute.time:
### Execution Time

For backup by month, week, or day, you can set a fine-grained incremental backup execution time, with the support for selection down to the minute level.

- Backup by month: If you set the execution time to 00:00 on the first day of each month, the incremental backup is executed at 00:00:00 on the first day of each month.
- Backup by week: If you set the execution time to 00:00 on Sunday and Tuesday of each week, the incremental backup is executed at 00:00:00 on Sunday and Tuesday of each week.
- Backup by day: If you set the execution time to 00:30, the incremental backup is executed at 00:30:00 every day.
