virtualization.appoint.vmCpuModel.toolti:
### VM CPU Mode

x86_64 architecture defaults to None, while aarch architecture defaults to Passthrough. This option Specifies whether to select the same CPU model as the host for a virtual machine. This configuration makes the virtual machine inherit some or all host CPU features that suit your business needs.

1. If you select "None", the CPU model of the VM is simulated via QEMU. In this mode, the VM inherits necessary host CPU features to a small degree. We recommend you select this mode if you need to migrate your VM.
2. If you select "Compatible", the CPU model of the VM is similar to or same as that of the host, such as Intel Haswell CPU. In this mode, the VM inherits many host CPU features. You can select this mode if you need to migrate your VM.
3. If you select "Passthrough", the CPU model as well as CPU features of the VM are the same as the CPU model and CPU features of the host. For example, both the VM and host support the extended page table extension, huge page, and virtualization features. Compared with the "None", "Compatible", and "Custom modes", VM in this mode has the most CPU features. You can select this mode if your business requires many features.
4. If you select "Custom" (a specific CPU model), the CPU model of the VM is set to the specified model. Different CPU models may have different CPU features.

virtualization.cluster.field.ha.enable.i:
### VM HA

Default: enabled. Specifies whether to automatically power on the virtual machine upon unexpected shutdown.

When enable the VM HA:

1. The virtual machine attempts to reboot automatically after it is unexpectedly shut down because of its own errors.

2. The virtual machine attempts to migrate to another host to power on according to its customized HA policy if errors occur to the compute, storage, or network resource it is residing on.

Note:

1. You can set a cluster-wide VM HA through Advanced Settings in a cluster. If you set the HA for an individual VM, the individual setting prevails over the cluster setting.
virtualization.cluster.field.hugepage.en: To enable hugepages, ensure all hosts in the cluster are in maintenance mode. Turning on/off this switch requires a host reboot to take effect.
Before enabling large pages of memory for a cluster, ensure all hosts within the cluster enter maintenance mode...

### HugePages

Default: disabled. When enabled, hugepages is enabled for all hosts in the cluster, with a size of 2 MB for each page. In addition, hugepage space is allocated to virtual machines.

Note:

1. Before you enable hugepages for a cluster, make sure that all hosts in the cluster are in maintenance mode.

2. If you enable hugepages for a cluster, you need to restart the hosts in the cluster for the change to take effect.

3. If hugepages is enabled for a cluster and you modify the memory of a host in the cluster, you need to re-enable hugepages and restart the host to make the hugepages feature take effect.

4. If you enable hugepages for a cluster, the host must reserve at least 4GB of memory. In addition, the rest of the memory in the host is allocated to hugepage memory.

5. Hugepage memory can be used only by virtual machines. You need to set a reasonable reserved memory size for hosts. A too-small reserved memory may cause system service exceptions of hosts. If you deploy a hyper-converged environment, you need to reserve memory for OSD processes, management node services, systems, and other processes. For example, if you use 5 OSD processes, we recommend that you set the reserved memory size to 50 GB. This number includes 25 GB for OSD processes, 15 GB for management node services and systems, and 10 GB for storage management.
### ignore_msrs Option

virtualization.instance.cpu.mode.tooltip:
### CPU Mode

Specifies whether to select the same CPU model as the host for a virtual machine. This configuration makes the virtual machine inherit some or all host CPU features that suit your business needs.
              
**For VM with x86_64 CPU architecture:**
              
1. Options: None, Compatible, Passthrough, and Custom Mode (a specific CPU model).
2. If you select "None", the CPU model of the VM is simulated via QEMU. In this mode, the VM inherits necessary host CPU features to a small degree. We recommend you select this mode if you need to migrate your VM.
3. If you select "Compatible", the CPU model of the VM  is similar to or same as that of the host, such as Intel Haswell CPU. In this mode, the VM inherits many host CPU features. You can select this mode if you need to migrate your VM.
4. If you select "Passthrough", the CPU model as well as CPU features of the VM are the same as the CPU model and CPU features of the host. For example, both the VM and host support the extended page table extension, huge page, and virtualization features. Compared with the "None", "Compatible", and "Custom modes", VM in this mode has the most CPU features. You can select this mode if your business requires many features.
5. If you select "Custom" (a specific CPU model), the CPU model of the VM is set to the specified model. Different CPU models may have different CPU features.
              
**For VM with aarch64 CPU architecture:**
              
1. Options: Inherit Cluster Setting (by default), None, Compatible, Passthrough, and Custom Mode (a specific CPU model).
2. If you select "Inherit Cluster Setting (by default)", the CPU model of the VM is consistent with the VM CPU model of the cluster where the VM resides.
3. If you select "Compatible", the CPU model of the VM  is similar to or same as that of the host, such as Intel Haswell CPU. In this mode, the VM inherits many host CPU features. You can select this mode if you need to migrate your VM.
4. If you select "Passthrough", the CPU model as well as CPU features of the VM are the same as the CPU model and CPU features of the host. For example, both the VM and host support the extended page table extension, huge page, and virtualization features. Compared with the "None", "Compatible", and "Custom modes", VM in this mode has the most CPU features. You can select this mode if your business requires many features.
5. If you select "Custom" (a specific CPU model), the CPU model of the VM is set to the specified model. Different CPU models may have different CPU features.
              
#### Note:
              
1. If you select "Passthrough", the VM will allow for virtualization. However, if you migrate a VM to a host whose CPU model is different from the current host, the migration may fail. In addition, the CPU utilization of the VM measured within the VM may differ from the CPU utilization measured from the host.
2. If you specifically set the CPU model of an individual virtual machine, the VM CPU model configured for the cluster will not take effect on that VM.
3. If you modify the CPU model, you need to reboot the VM to make the modification take effect.

### Type

Data storage includes the following types:

1. Local Storage: Uses the local disk directory on the host as data storage and can work with standalone image storage. The total capacity of a local storage is the sum of each host directory capacity.

2. NFS: Uses network file systems for storage, and can work with standalone image storage. The NFS directory is automatically mounted to all hosts.

4. SAN Storage: Uses LUN devices for storage and can work with standalone image storage. You can add one or more LUN devices. Note that you need to enter the unique disk identifier, such as UUID, WWN, and WWID.

### Storage Utilization

Displays the storage usage of the storage pool.

1. Storage Utilization = Physical Used / Physical Capacity

3. Safety Valve Capacity = Physical Capacity x (1 - Storage Utilization Threshold)

Displays the total allocatable amount and allocation status of the storage pool.

1. Storage Allocation Rate = Allocated : Overcommittable Total

3. Allocatable Total = Overcommittable Total × Overcommitment Ratio
4. Remaining Allocatable = Allocatable Total - Allocated

1. Attach an SSH public key to the VM instance, so that the root user can log in to it with the corresponding SSH private key.
2. Before you can attach SSH Key, make sure that:

    - The VM instance uses a Linux operating system.
    - The VM instance is running.
    - The VM instance has Qemu Guest Agent (QGA) installed and the QGA is running. You can install the QGA by installing the VM GuestTools. If installed through other methods, the QGA must be of 2.5 or later versions.

vm.action.set.biosSync.tip:
### Sync with Host BIOS Time

1. Specifies whether to sync Windows VM time with the host BIOS time. If enabled, Windows VM time is the same as that of the host. By default, the sync is enabled.

2. Note:

* If you enable time synchronization for a Windows VM instance, the VM time is synchronized with the host BIOS time automatically.
* If you disable time synchronization for a Windows VM instance, the VM time is not synchronized with the host BIOS time.
* If you modify the time synchronization setting for a Windows VM instance, the setting takes effect after the VM instance reboots.
* The time synchronization setting does not take effect on Linux VM instances.
* You can enable time sync in Global Setting for all Windows VM instances on the cloud. To enable time sync in Global Setting, set Sync with Host BIOS Time to Sync. By default, the time sync global setting is enabled.
* If you specifically set time sync for a Windows VM instance, the global setting does not take effect on the VM instance.
vm.action.set.biosSync.tip.modal:
1. If you modify the time synchronization setting for a Windows VM instance, the setting takes effect after the VM instance reboots.

2. The time synchronization setting does not take effect on Linux VM instances.
vm.action.set.biosSync.tip.set:
### Sync with Host BIOS Time

1. Specifies whether to sync Windows VM time with the host BIOS time. If enabled, Windows VM time is the same as that of the host. By default, the sync is enabled.

2. Note:

* If you enable time synchronization for a Windows VM instance, the VM time is synchronized with the host BIOS time automatically.
* If you disable time synchronization for a Windows VM instance, the VM time is not synchronized with the host BIOS time.
* If you modify the time synchronization setting for a Windows VM instance, the setting takes effect after the VM instance reboots.
* The time synchronization setting does not take effect on Linux VM instances.
* You can enable time sync in Global Setting for all Windows VM instances on the cloud. To enable time sync in Global Setting, set Sync with Host BIOS Time to Sync. By default, the time sync global setting is enabled.
* If you specifically set time sync for a Windows VM instance, the global setting does not take effect on the VM instance.
vm.action.set.cluster.ha.binding.tooltip:
### Set Cluster-Binding Policy
1. If set to true, the VM cross-cluster migrations are restricted. You can further define which migration operations are restricted through the cluster setting Resource Binding Policy.
2. If the cluster setting is Soft Binding:

   - The VM instance starts only in the current cluster by default, including starting triggered manually or triggered automatically by the VM HA or host maintenance mode. If no available hosts exist in the current cluster. The VM instance fails to start.
   - You can manually migrate the VM instance to another cluster through the Change Host or Change Host and Primary Storage action.
3. If the cluster setting is Hard Binding:

   - The VM instance can start only in the current cluster, including starting triggered manually or triggered automatically by the VM HA or host maintenance mode. If no available hosts exist in the current cluster. The VM instance fails to start.
   - You cannot manually migrate the VM instance to another cluster by exercising the Change Host or Change Host and Primary Storage action.
4. If set to false, the VM instance is not bound to the current cluster and can start in or be migrated to another cluster.

vm.action.set.hostname.Hostname.tooltip:
### Modify Hostname
1. The rules for setting Linux hostname and Windows hostname are different.
      *  Linux hostname: The hostname must be 2-60 characters in length, and can be uppercase, lowercase, digits, and hyphens (-). Note that a hostname cannot contain consecutive hyphens (-) and cannot start or end with hyphens (-).
      *  Windows hostname: The hostname must be 2-15 characters in length, and can be uppercase, lowercase, digits, and hyphens (-). Note that a hostname cannot contain consecutive hyphens (-), cannot start or end with hyphens (-), and cannot contain only digits.
2.  The modification takes effect through the VM GuestTools or DHCP service. However, the hostname of a Windows VM instance can be deployed and take effect only through the GuestTools.
      *  GuestTools: If the VM is running and installed the latest GuestTools, the hostname is deployed by the GuestTools and takes effect directly.
      *  DHCP service: If the VM instance is not running or does not have the latest GuestTools installed, the hostname is deployed by the DHCP service and takes effect after you restart the VM instance.
vm.action.set.hostname.alert.warning: The VM instance is not running or does not have GuestTools installed. The hostname is deployed by the DHCP service by default. Restart the VM instance to make the modification take effect. If you want to install GuestTools, click {ele}.
### Kernel Same-Page Merging
1. If you enable Kernel Same-Page Merging, the system detects whether this VM instance and other VM instances use virtual memory pages mapped to physical memory pages with identical content and re-maps these virtual memory pages to the same physical memory page, thus reducing duplicated occupation of physical memory resources.
2. To enable Kernel Same-Page Merging, make sure that the host memory overcommitment is higher than 1.0. You can set the memory overcommitment in the global setting or cluster advanced setting.
3. To enable Kernel Same-Page Merging, make sure that Cluster Hugepages is disabled in the cluster advanced setting.
4. If the VM instance is running important businesses, has the HA feature enabled, or is set with a high memory offering, we recommend that you do not enable Kernel Same-Page Merging for it.
vm.action.set.kvm.memory.recycling.tip:
### Memory Balloon
1. If you enable Memory Balloon, the system monitors in real-time the memory usage of VM instances and the host. If the workloads running on a VM instance decrease, the host reclaims unused memory of the VM instance when the physical memory usage is higher than 80%. If the workloads running on a VM instance increase, the host allocates necessary memory space to the VM instance. This dynamic reclaim and allocation mechanism makes sure the efficient use of host memory.
2. To enable Memory Balloon, make sure that the host memory overcommitment is higher than 1.0. You can set the memory overcommitment in the global setting or in the cluster advanced setting.
3. To enable Memory Balloon, make sure the cluster hugepages and VM vNUMA are disabled, and the VM instance has GuestTools installed.
4. If the VM instance is running important businesses or has the HA feature enabled, we recommend that you do not enable Memory Balloon for it.

vm.action.set.timeSync.tip:
### Time Synchronization

1. Specifies whether to sync VM time with the host system time. If enabled, the VM time is the same as that of the host system. By default, the sync is disabled.

2. Note:

* Before you enable the sync, make sure that Qemu Guest Agent (QGA) is installed on the VM and is running. You can install VMTools to install QGA.
* After you enable time synchronization for a VM, the VM time is synchronized with the host system time automatically.
* If you disable time synchronization for a VM, the VM time is not synchronized with the host system time.

vm.action.set.timeSync.tip.set:
### Sync with Host System Time

1. Specifies whether to sync VM time with the host system time. If enabled, the VM time is the same as that of the host system. By default, the sync is disabled.

2. Note:
* Before you enable the sync, make sure that QEMU Guest Agent (QGA) is installed on the VM instance and is running. You can install VM GuestTools to install QGA.
* Before you enable host system time sync, we recommend that you disable other time servers configured for the VM instance. 
* If you enable time synchronization for a VM instance, the VM time is synchronized with the host system time automatically on a regular basis.
* If you disable time synchronization for a VM instance, the VM time is not synchronized with the host system time.
* You can enable this time sync in Global Setting for all VM instances on the cloud. To enable time sync in Global Setting, turn on the Sync with Host System Time switch. By default, the time sync global setting is disabled.
* If you specifically set this time sync for a VM instance, the global setting does not take effect on the VM instance.

### Assign IPv4

If the network has IP Address Management and DHCP service disabled, the system does not allocate an IP address to the NIC automatically. To configure an IPv4, manually assign one on the Cloud or enter the VM operating system to configure.

1. If you assign an IPv4 address on the Cloud, note that

   - The IPv4 address cannot be occupied by another resource.
   - To make the IPv4 take effect, install VM GuestTools after the clone and sync configurations on the VM NIC action list. If the source VM has installed the latest GuestTools, the IPv4 takes effect directly after the creation.
2. If you enter the VM operating system to configure, you can install GuestTools for the VM instance to read this IPv4, thus making it displayed and managed by the Cloud. Note that

   - If you configure an IPv4 that has been occupied on the Cloud, this IPv4 cannot be read, and a conflict alarm will be triggered.
   - If you have assigned an IPv4 to the NIC on the Cloud, the Cloud displays the IPv4 assigned on the Cloud instead of the IPv4 configured in the VM instance by default. If you want to make the IPv4 configured in the VM displayed on the Cloud and overwrite that assigned on the Cloud, contact the official technical support.

### Failure Response Policy

Set an automatic response action for VM failures (Windows BSOD or Linux guest hang).

- No Action (default): Maintains current state without intervention.
- Reboot: Automatically reboots the VM. Stops after 5 reboot attempts within 30 minutes.
- Shut Down: Automatically shuts down the VM.

- Before setting this policy, install VMTools on the VM and make sure the VMTools is running properly.
- This policy takes effect immediately after configuration and does not require a VM reboot.

vm.create.cpuBind.tooltip:
### CPU Pinning
1. CPU pinning means making the system always assigns the specified host CPU (pCPU) to the VM CPU (vCPU). Three Policies are supported: Not Set, By NUMA Topology, and By Entry.

2. Not Set: Do not pin vCPUs to specified pCPUs. The system flexibly assigns pCPUs to vCPUs according to the resource scheduling conditions.

3. By NUMA Topology:

- Pins vCPUs to pCPUs based on the host pNUMA topology. You can implement Manual Pinning or Smart Pinning.
- Manual Pinning allows you to customize vCPU-pCPU binding for all vCPUs.
- Smart Pinning assigns a vCPU of a VM instance to a pCPU on a host pNUMA node by descending order of the pNUMA node ID. If all pCPUs on the pNUMA node are pinned, a pCPU on the next pNUMA node is to be pinned. If all pCPUs of the host are pinned but some vCPUs are not assigned with pCPUs, the system assigns the rest vCPUs with pCPUs from the pNUMA node with the maximum node ID again.
- You can pin a vCPU to one or more pCPU or pin one or more vCPU to a pCPU.
4. By Entry: Click Add CPU Pinning and enter the pinning rules manually. The system pins vCPUs to pCPUs according to the rules you entered. Enter a vCPU range in the left input box and a pCPU range in the right input box.
    - You can use an integer (-) between integers to indicate a vCPU/pCPU range.
    - You can use a caret (^) to exclude integers from a range.
    - You can add one or more ranges and excluding rules in an input box with commas (,) separating them.
   - Example: entering ”1“ in the left input box and  ”0-3,^2“ in the right input box means pinning vCPU1 to pCPU0, pCPU1, and pCPU3.
vm.create.field.cpuid.vendor.tooltip:
### CPU Vendor ID

If the virtual machine is running on a host with Hygon CPUs, it is recommended to set the VM's CPU vendor ID to AuthenticAMD to ensure compatibility with various operating systems and maintain normal VM operation. If set to None, certain operating systems may experience compatibility issues.
vm.create.field.dns.allocation.type.tool:
### Assign DNS

By default, the system automatically assigns DNS addresses, but you can manually specify a DNS.

1. Auto Allocated:
	- If DHCP is enabled on the distributed port group, DNS can be automatically assigned.
	- If DHCP is disabled on the distributed port group, DNS will be assigned and take effect through VMTools.
2. Manual Allocation: Manually configured DNS will be assigned and take effect through VMTools.

Notes:

- If VMTools is not installed on the VM, the DNS configuration will take effect after VMTools installation is completed.
- For Linux VMs, DNS can only be configured for NIC 1, with a maximum of 3 DNS addresses suppported.
- For Windows VMs, DNS can be configured for all NICs, with a maximum of 3 DNS addresses per NIC.
vm.create.field.macaddress.tooltip:
### MAC Address

By default, the system automatically assigns the MAC address. You can also specify a MAC address for your VM.

Note: If VMs are created in bulk, the assigned MAC address will default to be the start MAC address, and the rest available MAC addresses will be continuously assigned. When a MAC address has been occupied within the range, the corresponding VM cannot be created.
vm.create.field.networkConfig.tooltip:
### Network Configuration
1. Configure L3 networks for the VM instance. You can configure multiple L3 networks for a VM instance. Each L3 network corresponds to a NIC.
2. If the L3 network has DHCP service enabled, the NIC acquires an IP address in a dynamic mode (DHCP). The network configurations are automatically deployed to the NIC by DHCPClient.
3. If the L3 network has DHCP service disabled, the NIC acquires an IP address in a static mode (Static). To make the network configurations take effect, install GuestTools for the VM instance after it is created and manually sync the configurations to the NIC. If the VM image has encapsulated the latest GuestTools, the network configurations take effect directly.
vm.create.field.nicType.tooltip:
### NIC Model

Specifies the NIC model for the VM, with Linux defaulting to virtio and Windows to e1000.


* e1000: Emulates an Intel NIC to provide standard virtual networking suitable for basic connectivity needs.

* rtl8139: Emulates a Realtek NIC for scenarios that require compatibility with older operating systems or virtual machines, but not for high-performance or latency-sensitive application scenarios.

* virtio: A para-virtualized network driver with low CPU usage and high network throughput for high-performance network scenarios.

* SR-IOV: Virtualizes the physical NICs and cuts them into VF NICs and assigns them directly to VMs. This can achieve I/O performance close to that of physical devices and reduce the host CPU consumption.

* pcnet: Emulates an AMD PCnet NIC with excellent compatibility. Designed primarily for older guest operating systems such as Windows 2000/XP/NT 4.0 and legacy Linux distributions. Suitable for traditional system environments with low network demands.
vm.create.field.staticipv4.tooltip:
### IP Address

By default, the system automatically assigns the IP address. You can also specify an IP address for your VM.

Note: If VMs are created in bulk, the assigned IP address will default to be the start IP address, and the rest available IP addresses will be continuously assigned. When an IP address has been occupied or is insufficient within the range, the corresponding VM cannot be created.

vm.create.field.vmPortOff.tooltip:
### VMware I/O Port Simulation

1. Default: disabled. VMware IO port emulation allows KVM virtual machines to emulate IO ports in VMware virtualized environments, enabling KVM virtual machines to use the VMware IO port standard for compatibility with VMware virtualized environments.

2. Key purposes:

  * Migration & Compatibility: Allows for VM migration from VMware to a KVM environment, or to run both VMware and KVM VMs in a hybrid environment without significant configuration changes.
  * Testing & Development: Enables developers and testers to simulate a VMware environment using KVM VMs for application testing or configuration validation, eliminating the need for a separate VMware license.

vm.create.se.tooltip:
### SE-Based Encryption
1. SE (Security Element) is an embedded security IP core within the processor. It provides foundational software and application systems with secure, compliant, and standardized cryptographic support.
2. Enabling this feature allows an SE device from the host to be passed through to the VM instance. Currently, passthrough is supported for SE devices on hosts with LoongArch or Hygon processors.
   - LoongArch: If enabled, you can manually attach an SE device to the VM instance after the creation via the VM's detail page - Configuration Info - SE Device List.

vm.detail.field.cpuBind.tooltip:
### CPU Pinning
1. CPU pinning assigns the virtual CPUs (vCPUs) of a VM instance to specific host pCPUs, which improves VM performance. Two CPU pinning methods are supported: By NUMA Topology and By Entry.

2. By NUMA Topology:

- This method indicates that you pin vCPUs to pCPUs based on the host pNUMA topology. You can implement Manual Pinning or Smart Pinning.
- Manual Pinning allows you to customize vCPU-pCPU binding for all vCPUs.
- Smart Pinning assigns a vCPU of a VM instance to a pCPU on a host pNUMA node by descending order of the pNUMA node ID. If all pCPUs on the pNUMA node are pinned, a pCPU on the next pNUMA node is to be pinned. If all pCPUs of the host are pinned but some vCPUs are not assigned to pCPUs, each vCPU is assigned to a pCPU starting again from the pNUMA node with the maximum node ID.
- You can pin a vCPU to one or more pCPU or pin one or more vCPU to a pCPU.
- The utilization of each pCPU in the past 15 minutes is displayed. You can pin a vCPU to the optimal pCPU based on the utilization.
3. By Entry:

- Syntax:
  1. In the left input box, set a vCPU range. In the right input box, set a pCPU range. Range format: integer, hyphen , and caret (^). Use commas (,) to separate them.
  2. The vCPU range that you can set depends on the VM instance offering.
  3. The pCPU range that you can set depends on the pCPU quantity of the host.
- Example:
  1. In the left input box, enter 1. In the right input box, enter 0-3,^2. This example indicates that vCPU 1 is stringently associated with pCPU 0, pCPU 1, and pCPU 3, while ^ represents that vCPU 2 is excluded.

### CPU Pinning

CPU pinning associates the virtual CPUs (vCPUs) of a VM instance with host pCPUs stringently and allows you to allocate specific pCPUs for the VM instance, thus improving VM performances.

#### Pnning Format
1. In the left input box, set a vCPU range. In the right input box, set a pCPU range. Range format: integer, hyphen (-), and caret (^). Use commas to separate them.
2. The vCPU range depends on the vRouter offering attached to the VPC vRouter.

vm.field.cpuMode.tooltip:
### CPU Mode

Specifies whether to select the same CPU model as the host for a virtual machine. This configuration makes the virtual machine inherit some or all host CPU features that suit your business needs.

#### For VM with x86_64 CPU architecture: 

1. Options: Inherit Cluster Setting (by default), none, host-model, host-passthrough, and Custom (a specific CPU model).
2. If you select Inherit Cluster Setting (by default), the CPU model of the virtual machine is consistent with the VM CPU model of the cluster where the virtual machine resides.
3. If you select none, the CPU model of virtual machine is simulated via QEMU. In this mode, the virtual machine inherits necessary host CPU features to a small degree. We recommend you select this mode if you need to migrate your virtual machine.
4. If you select host-model, the CPU model of the virtual machine is similar to or same as that of the host, such as Intel Haswell CPU. In this mode, the virtual machine inherits many host CPU features. You can select this mode if you need to migrate your virtual machine.
5. If you select host-passthrough, the CPU model as well as CPU features of the virtual machine are the same as the CPU model and CPU features of the host. For example, both the virtual machine and host support the extended page table extension, huge page, and virtualization features. Compared with the none, host-model, and Custom modes, virtual machine in this mode has the most CPU features. You can select this mode if your business requires many features.
6. If you select Custom (a specific CPU model), the CPU model of the virtual machine is set to the specified model. Different CPU models may have different CPU features. Note that if your host CPU is Hygon and the OS of your virtual machine is an earlier version such as Windows Server 2012 R2 or Windows Server 2008 R2, you can select Hygon_Customized.

#### For VM with aarch64 CPU architecture: 

1. Options: Inherit Cluster Setting (by default), host-model, and host-passthrough, and Custom (a specific CPU model).
2. If you select Inherit Cluster Setting (by default), the CPU model of the virtual machine is consistent with the VM CPU model of the cluster where the virtual machine resides.
3. If you select host-model, the CPU model of the virtual machine is similar to or same as that of the host. In this mode, the virtual machine inherits many host CPU features. You can select this mode if you need to migrate your virtual machine.
4. If you select host-passthrough, the CPU model as well as CPU features of the virtual machine are the same as the CPU model and CPU features of the host. virtual machine in this mode has the most CPU features. You can select this mode if your business requires many features.
5. If you select Custom (a specific CPU model), the CPU model of the virtual machine is set to the specified model. Different CPU models may have different CPU features.

#### For VM with mips64el or loongarch64 architecture: 

You can only select a specific CPU model, and the CPU model of the virtual machine is set to the specified model.

#### Note: 

1. If you select host-passthrough, the virtual machine will allow for virtualization. However, if you migrate a virtual machine to a host whose CPU model is different from the current host, the migration may fail. In addition, the CPU utilization of the virtual machine measured within the instance may differ from the CPU utilization measured from the host.
2. Hygon_Customized is virtualized CPU model designed only for compating OS of eariler versions.
3. If you specifically set the CPU model of an individual virtual machine, the VM CPU model configured for the cluster or in the global settings will not take effect on that virtual machine.
4. If you modify the CPU model, you need to restart the virtual machine to make the modification take effect.
vm.field.crash.handle.strategy.tooltip:
### Error Handling Policy

 If your VM instance crashes, the VM instance is handled based on the configured policy. Three error handling polices are available: Preserve, Reboot, and Shutdown. Default: Preserve. This value indicates that if a Linux-based VM instance gets stuck or the blue-screen error occurs to a Windows-based VM instance, the system does not handle the error and the VM instance remains stuck or blue-screened. The value Reboot indicates that if a Linux-based VM instance gets stuck or the blue-screen error occurs to a Windows-based VM instance, the VM instance is automatically restarted. The value Shutdown indicates that if a Linux-based VM instance gets stuck or the blue-screen error occurs to a Windows-based VM instance, the VM instance is automatically shut down.

vm.field.designatedIp.no.ipam.ipv4.toolt:
### Assign IPv4
If the network has DHCP service and IP Address Management disabled, the system does not allocate an IP address to the NIC automatically. To configure an IPv4, manually assign one on the Cloud or enter the VM operating system to configure.

1. If you assign an IPv4 address on the Cloud, note that
   - The IPv4 address cannot be occupied by another resource.
   - To make the IPv4 take effect, install VM GuestTools after the creation and sync configurations on the VM NIC action list. If the VM image has encapsulated the latest GuestTools, the IPv4 takes effect directly after the creation.
   - If you create VM instances in bulk, the IPv4 address you enter is identified as the start IP and assigned to the first VM instance. The IPv4 addresses following it are continuously assigned to the rest VM instances. When an IPv4 has been occupied, the corresponding VM instance fails to be created.
2. If you enter the VM operating system to configure, you can install GuestTools for the VM instance to read this IPv4, thus making it displayed and managed by the Cloud. Note that
    - If you configure an IPv4 that has been occupied on the Cloud, this IPv4 cannot be read, and a conflict alarm will be triggered.
    - If you have assigned an IPv4 to the NIC on the Cloud, the Cloud displays the IPv4 assigned on the Cloud instead of that configured in the VM instance by default. If you want to make the IPv4 configured in the VM displayed and overwrite the IP assigned on the Cloud, contact the official technical support.

1. If you assign an IPv6 address on the Cloud, note that
   - The IPv6 address cannot be occupied by another resource.
   - To make the IPv6 take effect, install VM GuestTools after the creation and sync configurations on the VM NIC action list. If the VM image has encapsulated the latest GuestTools, the IPv6 takes effect directly after the creation.
   - If you create VM instances in bulk, the IPv4 address you enter is identified as the start IP and assigned to the first VM instance. The IPv6 addresses following it are continuously assigned to the rest VM instances. When an IPv6 has been occupied, the corresponding VM instance fails to be created.
2. If you enter the VM operating system to configure, you can install GuestTools for the VM instance to read this IPv6, thus making it displayed and managed by the Cloud. Note that
    - If you configure an IPv6 that has been occupied on the Cloud, this IPv6 cannot be read, and a conflict alarm will be triggered.
    - If you have assigned an IPv6 to the NIC on the Cloud, the Cloud displays the IPv4 assigned on the Cloud instead of that configured in the VM instance by default. If you want to make the IPv6 configured in the VM displayed and overwrite the IP assigned on the Cloud, contact the official technical support.

vm.field.externalMonitoring.tooltip:
### Internal Monitoring

Internal Monitoring is monitoring data that is obtained by the internal agent from the VM instance. To view internal monitoring data, install GuestTools for the VM instance in advance.

1. If the VM default network has a DHCP service enabled, the monitoring data is pushed to the host by the DHCP service by default.
2. If the VM default network does not have a DHCP service enabled or the DHCP service fails, the monitoring data is pushed by the QEMU Guest Agent (QGA) in the GuestTools. As soon as the DHCP service is recovered, the data is switched to be pushed by the DHCP service.

2. After you enable error inspection, if a VM instance crashes, the system handles the error based on the specified error handling policy. In addition, the VM Crash alarm is triggered.
3. If you enable error inspection for a Linux-based VM instance, the kdump module is disabled after you restart the instance.
vm.field.gpu.tooltip:
### GPU

1. Attach pGPUs or vGPUs to the VM instance.

   - pGPU: Passthrough a physical GPU device to the VM instance.
   - vGPU: Attach a vGPU device which is virtually divided from a pGPU to the VM instance.

2. Supports two GPU attachment policies:

   - By GPU Device: Select a GPU device and attach it directly to the VM instance.
   - By GPU Specification: Select a GPU specification and the system allocates GPU device(s) to the VM instance according to this specification. You can choose whether to make these GPU device(s) automatically detached when the VM is stopped.
      - Auto Detach: When the VM is stopped, these GPU device(s) are automatically detached. When the VM starts, the system re-allocates GPU device(s) to it according to the GPU specification.
      - Do not Auto Detach: When the VM is stopped, it keeps these GPU device(s) attached. However, if the VM is stopped unexpectedly, it cannot automatically start even though its HA mode is NeverStop.
vm.field.gpuDevice.tooltip:
### GPU Device

1. When creating VM instances, you can attach the GPU devices passed through by hosts to these VM instances.
2. Enable Intel VT-d or AMDIOMMU on host BIOS, and enable the IOMMU support in host kernels. Ensure that hosts can normally use the GPU passthrough feature.
3. Different types of GPU devices can be passed through to VM instances.
4. GPU devices cannot be passed through to VM instances across hosts.

vm.field.guestTools.tooltip:
### GuestTools
1. GuestTools consists of several drivers and tools that help improve VM performance and extend VM features.
     - GuestTools for Linux VM instances consists of QEMU Guest Agent (QGA) and internal agent.
     - GuestTools for Windows VM instances consists of QGA, internal agent, VirtIO driver, and Cloudbase-Init.

2. You can use the GuestTools to realize VM internal monitoring, configuration sync, and configuration read.
     - Internal monitoring: The internal agent in the GuestTools helps obtain monitoring data from the VM instance, including the data of the VM CPU, memory, and disk capacity.
     - Configuration sync: The QGA in the GuestTools helps deploy the network parameters and hostname you set on the Cloud to the VM instance to take effect.
     - Configuration read: The QGA in the GuestTools helps read the IP addresses configured in the VM instance and display them on the Cloud.
       - The system reads the IP addresses of NICs on L3 networks whose DHCP services are disabled.
       - The system displays the IP address it reads from the VM instance on the Cloud only if the NIC does not have an IP record on the Cloud. If the IP address configured in the VM instance differs from the Cloud record, an alarm is triggered to remind you to pay attention to it. However, this IP is neither displayed on the Cloud nor used to overwrite the Cloud record directly. In the following scenarios, the IP address configured in the VM instance may differ from the IP record on the Cloud:
            - You have assigned or specified an IP address for the NIC on the Cloud and then enter the VM instance to configure a different IP address or modify the existing IP address, which may cause an inconsistency between the NIC IP address and its IP record on the Cloud.
            - The Cloud has once read and displayed the NIC IP configured in the VM instance successfully, but you later enter the VM instance to modify the NIC IP, which may cause an inconsistency between the NIC IP address and its IP record on the Cloud.
            - In the scenarios above, if you want to display the NIC IP read from the VM instance on the Cloud and overwrite the origin IP record, making the Cloud record always consistent with the actual IP of the NIC, you can contact the official technical support.
       - If the NIC IP address you configured in the VM instance is occupied by another resource on the Cloud or is in the reserved network range of the L3 network, the IP is not read to the Cloud. In addition, an alarm is triggered to remind you to pay attention to it.
       - If the L3 network has IP Address Management enabled and the NIC IP address configured in the VM instance is not in the network range of the L3 network, the IP is not read to the Cloud. In addition, an alarm is triggered to remind you to pay attention to it.
       - If you configure more than one IPv6 address for a NIC, the system reads only the first queryable IPv6 address.
       - If the VM instance uses a Windows OS, the system does not read the IP addresses (169.254/16) generated by APIPA.
       - If the NIC uses an IPv6 address, the system does not read the local link address (FE80::/64) automatically generated.

### HA Mode
Specifies whether to make the VM instance automatically reboot if an unexpected stopping or error occurs. Valid values: None and NeverStop.

1. None: The VM instance does not reboot automatically after an unexpected stopping or error.

2. NeverStop:

   - The VM instance attempts to reboot automatically after it is unexpectedly stopped because of its own errors.
   - The VM instance attempts to migrate to another host automatically if errors occur to the compute, network, or storage resource it is residing on.
   - The VM instance does not reboot automatically if it is stopped manually or through a scheduled job.
   -  Note: If you choose NeverStop, make sure that you have enabled HA Policy in Platform Setting. Otherwise, the NeverStop mode does not take effect.

### Password

1. For Linux VM instances:
- The fixed username is root. After you set a password, you can SSH to a running VM instance by using the password.
- Before you set a password, make sure that Cloud-Init is installed for the VM image. Recommended Cloud-Init versions: 0.7.9, 17.1, 19.4, 19.4, and later.
- If a VM instance runs CentOS, you can install Cloud-Init by running the yum install cloud-init command.

2. For Windows VM instances:
- The fixed username is administrator. After you set a password, you can log in to a running VM instance by using the password.
- Before you set a login password, make sure that Cloudbase-Init is installed for the VM image. Recommended Cloudbase-Init version: 0.9.11.
- For more information about how to install Cloudbase-Init, see the [Cloudbase Documentation](https://cloudbase.it/cloudbase-init).
3. Enter letters, digits, and special characters. Supported special characters include -`=[];',./~!@#$%^&*()_+|{}:"<>?

4. You can enable VM Password Strength in Global Setting to set password strength.

5. After you set the password, do not set it again via User Data to avoid conflicts of duplicate operations.

6. If you set the password, the password is displayed on User Data of the VM details page. Secure your password as needed.

vm.field.userData.tooltip:
### User Data

1. You can upload user-defined parameters or scripts to customize configurations for VM instances or to accomplish specific tasks.
2. Before you import user data, make sure that both the user data network service and the DHCP network service work as expected.
3. For Linux VM instances:
    - Before you import user data, make sure that Cloud-Init is installed for the VM image. Recommended Cloud-Init versions: 0.7.9, 17.1, 19.4, 19.4, and later.
    - If you set the VM password in "Login Method", do not set it again in User Data. Otherwise, a conflict may occur.
    - If you set the VM hostname both the Hostname input box and User Data. The value in the User Data takes effect.
4. For Windows VM instances:
    - Before you import user data, make sure that Cloudbase-Init is installed for the VM image. Recommended Cloudbase-Init version: 0.9.11.
    - We recommend that you do not modify the default username in Cloudbase-Init. If the Cloudbase-Init default user name is the same as the VM OS username, Cloudbase-Init generates a random password for this OS user and overwrites the password you set.
    -  If you set the VM password in "Login Method", do not set it again in User Data. Otherwise, a conflict may occur.
    - Do not set a hostname for a Windows VM instance in UserData during the creation. If you set one, this hostname does not take effect after the creation. To set the hostname for a Windows VM instance, finish the creation and install a GuestTools for the VM instance first.
5. If you set the login password in user data, the password is displayed on User Data of the VM details page. Secure your password as needed.

Note: You cannot use User Data if the VM instance uses an SR-IOV VF NIC.

#### **Example**
The following example describes how to import user data for a Linux VM instance:
```
#cloud-config
users:
 - name: test
   shell: /bin/bash
   groups: users
   sudo: ['ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL']
   ssh-authorized-keys:
       - ssh-rsa AAAAB3NzaC1LXCJfjroD1lT root@10-0-0-18
bootcmd:
 - mkdir /tmp/temp
write_files:
 - path: /tmp/cloud_config
   content: |
       Hello,world!
   permissions: '0755'
fqdn: Perf-test
disable_root: false
ssh_pwauth: yes
chpasswd:
  list: |
      root:word
  expire: False
runcmd:
 - echo ls -l / >/root/list.sh
```
The script above can do the following:

1. Create a user named test and use the ssh-key method when a VM instance is created.
2. Enter the /etc/hosts file, create a directory named /tmp/temp, and then create a file and write data in the file.
3. Set a hostname, enable the root user and SSH login, and then change the root password.
4. Run the echo ls -l command.

vm.field.vm.ha.across.clusters.title.too:
### Bind with Cluster

1. If set to true, the VM cross-cluster migrations are restricted. You can further define which migration operations are restricted through the cluster setting Resource Binding Policy.
2. If the cluster setting is Soft Binding:
    - The VM instance starts only in the current cluster by default, including starting triggered manually or triggered automatically by the VM HA or host maintenance mode. If no available hosts exist in the current cluster. The VM instance fails to start.
    - You can manually migrate the VM instance to another cluster through the Change Host or Change Host and Primary Storage action.
3. If the cluster setting is Hard Binding:
   - The VM instance can start only in the current cluster, including starting triggered manually or triggered automatically by the VM HA or host maintenance mode. If no available hosts exist in the current cluster. The VM instance fails to start.
   - You cannot manually migrate the VM instance to another cluster by exercising the Change Host or Change Host and Primary Storage action.
4. If set to false, the VM instance is not bound to the current cluster and can start in or be migrated to another cluster.
vm.field.vmGroup.tooltip:

2. The scheduling policies associated with a VM scheduling group can be classified into the following four types: VM Exclusive from Each Other, VM Affinitive to Each Other, VMs Affinitive to Hosts, and VMs Exclusive from Hosts.

vm.field.vnuma.tooltip:
### vNUMA
1. vNUMA uses CPU pinning to passthrough the topology of associated host physical NUMA (pNUMA) nodes to a VM instance. Then a topology of virtual NUMA (vNUMA) nodes is generated for the VM instance. This topology enables a CPU on a vNUMA node of the VM instance to access its own local memory and thus improves VM performance.

2. vNUMA is disabled by default. Before you can enable vNUMA, make sure that Instance Offering Online Modification and Memory Balloon on the details page of the VM instance is disabled.

3. vNUMA functions based on CPU pinning. Before you enable vNUMA, make sure:

- All virtual CPUs (vCPUs) of the VM instance are pinned to physical CPUs (pCPUs) of the host. 
- The pCPUs pinned by a vCPU belong to the same pNUMA node.
4. Note:

- If you enable vNUMA for the VM instance, before you hot migrate the VM instance across hosts, make sure that the pNUMA architecture of the destination host is consistent with that of the source host.
- If you enable vNUMA for the VM instance and then hot migrate the VM instance across hosts and primary storages, the VM instance will be migrated only to a host that has the same pNUMA architecture of the source host.
- If you enable vNUMA for the VM instance, you cannot configure CPU pinning on the details page of the VM instance.
- If you enable vNUMA for the VM instance, you cannot online modify the instance offering on the details page of the VM instance.

2. You can enable or disable anti-spoofing for all VM instances on the Cloud. If you specify this setting specifically for a VM instance, this global setting does not take effect on the VM instance.

3. Anti-Spoofing Mode is not compatible with IPv6 addresses. We recommend that you do not enable it for a VM instance that is using an IPv6 address for this will interrupt the VM IPv6 communications.

- Destination Format: The migrated volume uses the default provisioning type of the destination primary storage.
- Thin Provision: The volume is set to thin provision after migration.
- Thick Provision: The volume is set to thick provision after migration.

### Kernel Same-Page Merging
1.  If you enable Kernel Same-Page Merging, the system detects whether this VM instance and other VM instances use virtual memory pages mapped to physical memory pages with identical content and re-maps these virtual memory pages to the same physical memory page, thus reducing duplicated occupation of physical memory resources.
2. To enable Kernel Same-Page Merging, make sure that the host memory overcommitment is higher than 1.0. You can set the memory overcommitment in the global setting or cluster advanced setting.
3. To enable Kernel Same-Page Merging, make sure that Cluster Hugepages is disabled in the cluster advanced setting.
4. If the VM instance is running important businesses, has the HA feature enabled, or is set with a high memory offering, we recommend that you do not enable Kernel Same-Page Merging for it.
vm.flatte.action.kvm.memory.recycling:
### Memory Balloon
1. If you enable Memory Balloon, the system monitors in real-time the memory usage of VM instances and the host. If the workloads running on a VM instance decrease, the host reclaims unused memory of the VM instance when the physical memory usage is higher than 80%. If the workloads running on a VM instance increase, the host allocates necessary memory space to the VM instance. This dynamic reclaim and allocation mechanism makes sure the efficient use of host memory.
2. To enable Memory Balloon, make sure that the host memory overcommitment is higher than 1.0. You can set the memory overcommitment in the global setting or in the cluster advanced setting.
3. To enable Memory Balloon, make sure the cluster hugepages and VM vNUMA are disabled, and the VM instance has GuestTools installed.
4. If the VM instance is running important businesses or has the HA feature enabled, we recommend that you do not enable Memory Balloon for it.
vm.flatte.action.tooltip:
### Flatten

Flatten refers to merging multiple snapshots of selected resources to improve resource performance and data security. By flattening, you can unlink the dependency between linked clone VM instances/volumes and source VM instances/volumes to achieve data independence.

#### Note that:

1. Flatten may take a long time if the selected resources have relatively large data.
2. During flattening, operations on VM instances/volumes will be conducted after the flattening is completed.
3. After flattened, storage space occupied by cloned VM instances/volumes may increase.
4. Flattening a VM instance also flattens the data volumes attached to the VM instance. If you flatten a VM instance that has shared volumes attached, the shared volumes will not be flattened.

#### Restrictions:

1. You can flatten a VM instance that is in the running/stopped/paused state.
2. You cannot flatten a disabled volume or shared volume.
3. You cannot flatten a VM instance that has a running CDP task and whose primary storage is not Ceph.
4. You cannot flatten a volume if the VM instance attached by the volume has a running CDP task and the primary storage of the volume is not Ceph.

vm.migrate.action.change.host.tooltis:
### Change Host

Migrating a VM instance to another host. This action changes only the host where the VM instance runs.

#### Hot Migration

1. The VM instance needs to be in the running state.

2. Supported primary storage types: LocalStorage, NFS, SMP, Ceph, SharedBlock, and Vhost.

    - If the VM instance uses a LocalStorage, you need to enable the Change Host Online on Local Storage in the Global Setting. Windows VMs on LocalStorage cannot be migrated.

3. Before you hot migrate the VM instance with the VF NIC attached, note that:

    - Make sure the VM instance has GuestTools (QGA) installed and the QGA is running.
    - VF NIC VM migration may fail if the internal driver version of the VM is too low. Check and update the driver version as needed.

4. Before you hot migrate a VM instance, detach the data volumes, ISOs, or peripheral devices (if any) from the VM instance first.

5. If vNUMA is enabled for a VM instance, before you hot migrate the VM instance, make sure that the pNUMA architecture of the destination host is consistent with that of the source host.

6. If a VM instance has a block device attached and is deployed as the master node of a Windows fail-over cluster, hot migrating the VM instance may make the fail-over cluster unavailable. Proceed with caution.

7. If the VM instance is associated with VM scheduling policies, hot migration may cause conflicts during the execution of the policies. Proceed based on your needs.

8. If the migration is blocked because the VM instance has high I/O operations for a long time, you can enable auto-convergence to ensure the migration is successful. If your applications are performance sensitive, we do not recommend that you enable auto-converge.

#### Cold Migration

1. The VM instance needs to be in the stopped state.

2. Supported primary storage type: LocalStorage.

3. Before you cold migrate a VM instance, detach the data volumes, ISOs, or peripheral devices (if any) from the VM instance first.


For more information about changing host, refer to related documentation in the help center.
vm.migrate.action.change.hostAndPrimaryS:
Cannot Change Host and Primary Storage, possibly because:

1. The VM instance does not install GuestTools (QGA).
2. The GuestTools (QGA) are not functioning properly.

### Change Host and Primary Storage

Migrating a VM instance to another host and primary storage. 

#### Hot Migration

- Supported Primary Storage

  1. Hot migration across primary storage of the same type: Ceph↔Ceph, NFS↔NFS, SharedBlock↔SharedBlock, LocalStorage↔LocalStorage.

  2. Hot migration across primary storage of different types: Ceph↔SharedBlock, LocalStorage↔SharedBlock, LocalStorage↔Ceph, LocalStorage↔NFS, SharedBlock↔NFS, Ceph↔NFS.

  3. Hot migration across Ceph pools within the same Ceph storage.

- Notes

  1. The VM instance needs to be in the running state.

  2. If a shared volume is attached to the VM instance, the shared volume cannot be migrated.

  3. If vNUMA is enabled for a VM instance, the VM instance will be migrated only to a host that has the same pNUMA architecture of the source host.
  
  4. Before you hot migrate the VM instance with the VF NIC attached, note that:

      - Make sure the VM instance has GuestTools (QGA) installed and the QGA is running.

      - VF NIC VM migration may fail if the internal driver version of the VM is too low. Check and update the driver version as needed.

  5. Snapshots of the VM instance to be migrated will not be saved after the hot migration.

  6. For hot migration across primary storage of the same type and different types, you can only migrate the entire VM instance. For hot migration across Ceph pools within the same Ceph storage, you can migrate the root volumes only or the entire VM instance.

  7. Before you hot migrate a VM instance across Ceph primary storages, make sure that the monitor nodes of these two Ceph primary storages can communicate with each other.

  8. If you hot migrate a VM instance across Ceph primary storages, you can specify a root volume pool or data volume pool for the volumes to be migrated.

  9. If you hot migrate a VM instance from a SharedBlock, Localstorage, or an NFS primary storage to a Ceph primary storage, you can specify a root volume pool or data volume pool for the volumes to be migrated.

#### Cold Migration

- Supported Primary Storage

  1. Cold migration across primary storage of the same type: Ceph↔Ceph, NFS↔NFS.

  2. Cold migration across Ceph pools within the same Ceph storage.

- Notes

  1. The VM instance needs to be in the stopped state and detach all its data volumes.

  2. If a shared volume is attached to the VM instance, the shared volume cannot be migrated.

  3. For Ceph↔Ceph cold migration: If you set a cold migration network for the target primary storage, the VM instance is migrated through the cold migration network. Otherwise, the VM instance is migrated through the management network.

  4. For NFS↔NFS cold migration: The destination NFS primary storage can be attached to the cluster where the VM instance to be migrated is located.

For more information about changing host and primary storage, refer to related documentation in the help center.
Cannot Change Primary Storage, possibly because:

1. You can migrate a VM instance that is in the running, paused, or stopped state.
2. The primary storage that the VM instance uses does not support migration.
3. The VM instance has ISO, shared volumes, LUNs, or other peripheral devices attached.
4. For VM instance that uses VF NICs, you need to install the GuestTools (QGA) first and make sure the GuestTools (QGA) are functioning properly.

### Change Primary Storage

Migrating a VM instance to another primary storage. This action only migrates valid data and the migrated VM instance follows the provisioning type of the target primary storage.

#### Supported Storage

1. SharedBlock ↔SharedBlock hot migration
2. SharedBlock ↔SharedBlock cold migration
3. SharedBlock ↔Ceph hot migration

#### Notes

1. Before hot migration, the VM instance needs to be in the running state. Before cold migration, make sure the VM instance is stopped.

2. Make sure that the source and destination primary storages are in the same cluster.

3. If a shared volume is attached to the VM instance, the shared volume cannot be migrated.

4. Before you hot migrate a VM instance, detach the ISOs or block devices from the VM instance first.

5. Before you hot migrate the VM instance with the VF NIC attached, note that:

    - Make sure the VM instance has GuestTools (QGA) installed and the QGA is running.
    - VF NIC VM migration may fail if the internal driver version of the VM is too low. Check and update the driver version as needed.

6. Snapshots of the VM instance to be migrated will not be saved after the hot migration.

7. If you hot migrate a VM instance from a SharedBlock primary storage to a Ceph primary storage, you can specify a root volume pool or data volume pool for the volumes to be migrated.

For more information about changing primary storage, refer to related documentation in the help center.

vm.numa.modal.title:
### vNUMA

1. The virtual NUMA (vNUMA) topology is generated based on CPU pinning. The topology passthroughs the topology of associated host pNUMA nodes.

2. The vCPUs that pin pCPUs residing on the same pNUMA node  form a vNUMA node. Therefore, each vNUMA node is associated with a pNUMA node.

3. Total Memory: The total amount of local memory that a virtual CPU (vCPU) can access from the vNUMA node where it resides.

 

### pNUMA

1. All pNUMA nodes that associate with the virtual machine are displayed.

2. Total Memory: The total amount of local memory that a physical CPU (pCPU) can access from the pNUMA node where it resides.

3. Free Memory: The amount of free local memory that a physical CPU (pCPU) can access from the pNUMA node where it resides.

4. Both the total memory and free memory are measured based on physical hardware resources.

### Remote Retention Policy

Set the policy how remote backup data is retained. The backup data can be retained permanently, by quantity, or by time (day/week/month).

- Permanently: The remote backup data will not be cleared automatically.
- By quantity: Retains a minimum of 1 remote incremental backup data and 1 remote full backup data.
- By time: Retains a minimum of 1 day of remote backup data.

Note: For data generated beyond the retention policy, only the backup records are deleted, which does not affect the data security.

vm.setting.normal.config.hostname.icon.t:
### Hostname

1. The rules for setting Linux hostname and Windows hostname are different.

- Linux hostname: The hostname must be 2-60 characters in length, and can be uppercase, lowercase, digits, and hyphens (-). Note that a hostname cannot contain consecutive hyphens (-) and cannot start or end with hyphens (-).
- Windows hostname: The hostname must be 2-15 characters in length, and can be uppercase, lowercase, digits, and hyphens (-). Note that a hostname cannot contain consecutive hyphens (-), cannot start or end with hyphens (-), and cannot contain only digits.

2. The modification takes effect through the VMTools or DHCP service. However, the hostname of a Windows VM can be deployed and take effect only through the VMTools.

- VMTools: If the VM is running and installed the latest VMTools, the hostname is deployed by the VMTools and takes effect directly.
- DHCP service: If the VM is not running or does not have the latest VMTools installed, the hostname is deployed by the DHCP service and takes effect after you reboot the VM.

vm.snapshot.glossary:
### VM Snapshot
1. Before you perform a business-sensitive operation, you can create a snapshot for a VM instance to record the state of its root volume, data volume, and VM memory. This allows rollback in case of breakdowns.

2. To back up data for the long term, you can use a backup service.

3. You can create snapshots for a running, paused, or stopped VM instance.

4. You cannot create a snapshot group for a VM instance to which a shared volume is attached.

5. VM snapshots do not occupy the storage space of Ceph primary storage. The displayed snapshot size indicates the storage capacity occupied by the VM root volume at the creation time of the snapshot.

6. More information about various editions of Ceph primary storage:
   - The sizes of VM snapshots in Open-source Ceph Hammer series and Ceph Enterprise 3.2.0 or earlier are inaccessible.
   -   The sizes of VM snapshots in Ceph Enterprise 3.2.0 or later may be inaccessible due to the format of RBD images.

### SE Device
1. This list displays SE devices attached to the VM instance.
2. SE (Security Element) is an embedded security IP core within the processor. It provides foundational software and application systems with secure, compliant, and standardized cryptographic support.

vm.vnuma.field.cpuBind.tooltip:
### CPU Pinning
1. CPU pinning assigns the virtual CPUs (vCPUs) of a VM instance to specific host pCPUs, which improves VM performance. Two CPU pinning methods are supported: By NUMA Topology and By Entry.

2. By NUMA Topology:

- This method indicates that you pin vCPUs to pCPUs based on the host pNUMA topology. You can implement Manual Pinning or Smart Pinning.
- Manual Pinning allows you to customize vCPU-pCPU binding for all vCPUs.
- Smart Pinning assigns a vCPU of a VM instance to a pCPU on a host pNUMA node by descending order of the pNUMA node ID. If all pCPUs on the pNUMA node are pinned, a pCPU on the next pNUMA node is to be pinned. If all pCPUs of the host are pinned but some vCPUs are not assigned to pCPUs, each vCPU is assigned to a pCPU starting again from the pNUMA node with the maximum node ID.
- You can pin a vCPU to one or more pCPU or pin one or more vCPU to a pCPU.
- The utilization of each pCPU in the past 15 minutes is displayed. You can pin a vCPU to the optimal pCPU based on the utilization.
3. By Entry:

- Syntax:
  1. In the left input box, set a vCPU range. In the right input box, set a pCPU range. Range format: integer, hyphen , and caret (^). Use commas (,) to separate them.
  2. The vCPU range that you can set depends on the VM instance offering.
  3. The pCPU range that you can set depends on the pCPU quantity of the host.
- Example:
  1. In the left input box, enter 1. In the right input box, enter 0-3,^2. This example indicates that vCPU 1 is stringently associated with pCPU 0, pCPU 1, and pCPU 3, while ^ represents that vCPU 2 is excluded.

vmClone.field.cloneType.tooltip:
### Clone Method

1. Full Clone: The cloned VM is independent of the source VM, and the performance is completely unaffected after cloning, but the VM starts slow.
2. Instant Full Clone: The cloned VM starts quickly, the VM is eventually independent of the source VM, and the performance is completely unaffected after cloning.

#### Note:

1. When you use Instant Full Clone to clone a VM, the system automatically performs Flatten to eventually achieve data independence. During flattening, operations on VMs/disks will be conducted after the flattening is completed.
vmClone.field.count.description: When you clone VMs in bulk, the names of these VMs will be followed by -1, -2, -3, and so forth to distinguish these VMs.
vmClone.field.primaryStorage.tooltip:
### Data Storage
By default, the system automatically assigns data storage for cloned virtual machines, but you can manually specify a data storage.

1. Auto Allocated: The cloned VM and its disks will use the same data storage as the source VM and its disks.
2. Manual Allocation: The cloned VM and its disks will use the data storage you specify.

Notes:

1. You can only specify data storage when using full clone.
2. If Disk 1 of the source VM uses local storage while the other disks use different types of data storage, the clone operation will fail if local storage is unavailable.
3. When specifying SAN storage as the data storage, you can set separate provisioning methods for Disk 1 and other disks.
vmClone.field.stopAfterClone.checkbox: Auto-start the cloned VM instances after cloning
vmClone.field.volumeAllocateStrategy.too:
### Storage Allocation Policy

1. System Allocation: The Cloud allocates a primary storage based on your selected clone method.
     - Full Clone:
       - Clone without attached volumes: The Cloud automatically allocates a primary storage.
       - Clone attached volumes: The Cloud allocates a primary storage consistent with that of the source VM instance/volume.
    -  Instant Full Clone/Linked Clone: The Cloud allocates a primary storage consistent with that of the source VM instance/volume.


2. Manual Allocation: You can select the primary storage as needed.

#### Note that:

1. Instant full clone and linked clone support system allocation only.

vmNic.action.set.ip.tooltip:
### Set Network and IP Address

1. Allows you to modify the L3 network and IP address used by the NIC. You can make the modification when the VM instance is running or stopped. If the VM instance is running, the network type cannot be changed.
2. Different networks support different IP allocation methods:
    - A network with IP Address Management enabled supports two IP allocation methods: Assign IP and By IP Allocation Policy.
    - A network with IP Address Management disabled supports only Assign IP. Or, you can configure an IP address in the VM operating system. The IP address configured in the VM operating system can be read to the Cloud through the VM GuestTools.
3. After the modification, you can make it take effect through VM GuestTools of the latest version or by restarting the DHCP Client.
    - Through VM GuestTools:
        - If the VM instance has the GuestTools of the latest version installed, the network and IP address settings are automatically configured on the NIC and takes effect directly.
        - If the VM instance does not have the GuestTools of the latest version installed, you can install one after the modification and sync NIC configurations on the VM NIC action list to make the modification take effect.
    - By restarting DHCP Client:
        - Linux VM instance:
            - If the network is not managed by NetworkManager, run the following command: dhclient -r ${ifname}; dhclient ${ifname}
            - If the network is managed by NetworkManager, run the following command: nmcli c up ${ifname}
        - Windows VM instance: Enter the command line tool and run the following command: ipconfig /release && ipconfig /renew
        - Restarting DHCP Client interrupts the VM network temporarily. The network auto-resumes after the DHCP Client is restarted successfully.
        - This method does not apply to L3 networks with DHCP service disabled.

vmSchedulingRule.field.excuteMode.toolti:
### Execution Mechanism

A VM scheduling policy can be executed based on either of the following mechanisms:

- Hard: Virtual machines are forcibly assigned hosts based on the associated VM scheduling policies. For example, if you associate the VM Exclusive from Each Other policy with a VM scheduling group and select the Hard mechanism for the policy, any two of the virtual machines in the scheduling group are not allowed to run on the same host. If no host is available to be scheduled based on the policy for a virtual machine, the virtual machine will end up failure upon startup.

- Soft: Virtual machines are primarily assigned hosts based on the associated VM scheduling policies. For example, if you associate the VM Exclusive from Each Other policy with a VM scheduling group and select the Soft mechanism for the policy, any two of the virtual machines in the scheduling group will primarily not run on the same host. If no host is available to be scheduled based on the policy for a virtual machine, the virtual machine will attempt to run on a host that does not satisfy the policy.
vmSchedulingRule.field.excuteState.toolt:
### Execution Status

A VM scheduling policy may have one of the following three status during execution:

- Normal: All virtual machines associated with the VM scheduling policy are scheduled based on the policy.
- Conflicted: Some virtual machines associated with the VM scheduling policy are not running on hosts assigned based on the policy.
- Inactive: The VM scheduling policy is disabled. It does not take effect on the associated virtual machines.

vmSchedulingRule.field.type.tooltip:
### Type

Supports four types of VM scheduling policies: VM Exclusive from Each Other, VM Affinitive to Each Other, VMs Affinitive to Hosts, and VMs Exclusive from Hosts. Each policy has two execution mechanisms: Hard and Soft. Virtual machines are scheduled based on their associated scheduling policies and policy execution mechanisms:

- VM Exclusive from Each Other: Virtual machines in the same VM scheduling group should not/must not run on the same host.
- VM Affinitive to Each Other: Virtual machines in the same VM scheduling group should/must run on the same host.
- VMs Exclusive from Hosts: Given any one of the virtual machines in a VM scheduling group and any one of the hosts in a host scheduling group, the virtual machine should not/must not run the host.
- VMs Affinitive to Hosts: Given any one of the virtual machines in a VM scheduling group and any one of the hosts in a host scheduling group, the virtual machine should/must run the host.

2. The scheduling policies associated with a VM scheduling group can be classified into the following four types: VM Exclusive from Each Other, VM Affinitive to Each Other, VMs Affinitive to Hosts, and VMs Exclusive from Hosts.

### Change Primary Storage

You can migrate a volume to another primary storage.

1. You can migrate a data volume across primary storages of the same type, including Ceph, NFS, and SharedBlock.

    - To migrate a data volume across Ceph primary storages or NFS primary storages, make sure that the data volume is not attached to a VM instance.

    - You can migrate a volume from a SharedBlock primary storage after you attach the volume to a VM instance that is in the running or stopped state.

    - To migrate a data volume across Ceph primary storages, make sure that the Mon nodes of these two Ceph primary storages are connected with each other.

    - When you migrate a data volume across Ceph primary storages, you can specify a data volume pool for the volume to be migrated.

    - To migrate a data volume across NFS primary storages, make sure that the destination NFS primary storage can be attached to the cluster where the data volume resides.

    - To migrate a data volume across SharedBlock primary storages, make sure that the destination SharedBlock primary storage can be attached to the cluster where the data volume resides.

2. If a data volume uses a Ceph primary storage, you can migrate the data volume across different Ceph pools within the Ceph primary storage. Make sure that the data volume is not attached to a VM instance.
The owner of the volume is different from the owner of the instance. If you attach the volume to the instance, the VM instance may become invisible to the tenant/sub-account, which makes the tenant unable to manage the VM instance. Proceed with caution.

volume.field.type.tooltip:
### Volume Mode

#### Classic Volume

A classic volume can be created on all types of primary storage.

#### Shared Volume

A shared volume is essentially the volume that can be attached to multiple VM instances for use, which is similar to a physical disk in that the disk can be attached to multiple physical servers, and each server can read data from and write data into the disk.

Note:

1. A shared volume can be created on Ceph or SharedBlock primary storage. However, you cannot create a thin-provisioned shared volume on SharedBlock primary storage.
2. By default, VirtioSCSI is enabled for shared volumes.
3. If you simply attach a shared volume to multiple VM instances, files cannot be shared between VM instances. Build a shared file system if you need to share files between VM instances.

### Volume Provisioning Type

#### Configure the provisioning type of volumes after a migration. 

- Source Format: The migrated volume retains the same provisioning type as the source volume.
- Destination Format: The migrated volume uses the default provisioning type of the destination primary storage.
- Thin Provision: The volume is set to thin provision after migration.
- Thick Provision: The volume is set to thick provision after migration.

volume.flatte.action.tooltip:
### Flatten

Flatten refers to merging multiple snapshots of selected resources to improve resource performance and data security. By flattening, you can unlink the dependency between linked clone VM instances/volumes and source VM instances/volumes to achieve data independence.

#### Note that:

1. Flatten may take a long time if the selected resources have relatively large data.
2. During flattening, operations on VM instances/volumes will be conducted after the flattening is completed.
3. After flattened, storage space occupied by cloned VM instances/volumes may increase.
4. Flattening a VM instance also flattens the data volumes attached to the VM instance. If you flatten a VM instance that has shared volumes attached, the shared volumes will not be flattened.

#### Restrictions:

1. You can flatten a VM instance that is in the running/stopped/paused state.
2. You cannot flatten a disabled volume or shared volume.
3. You cannot flatten a VM instance that has a running CDP task and whose primary storage is not Ceph.
4. You cannot flatten a volume if the VM instance attached by the volume has a running CDP task and the primary storage of the volume is not Ceph.

### Volume Snapshot
1. Before you perform a business-sensitive operation, you can create a snapshot for a VM instance to record the state of its root volume and data volume. This allows rollback in case of breakdowns.

2. To back up data for the long term, you can use a backup service.

3. You can create snapshots for a running, paused, or stopped VM instance.

5. More information about various editions of Ceph primary storage:
    - The sizes of volume snapshots in Open-source Ceph Hammer series and Ceph Enterprise 3.2.0 or earlier are inaccessible.

vpc.vrouter.action.set.snat.field.snat.t:
### SNAT
1. By default, SNAT is enabled for the default public network and disabled for the non-default public networks associated with the VPC vRouter.   
   - If you enable SNAT for the default public network, VM instances in the corresponding VPC network can directly access the Internet via the public network.  
   - If you enable SNAT for a non-default public network, VM instances in the corresponding VPC network can access the VM instances in the public network. 
 
2. If you modify the SNAT setting for the public network, the modification takes effect immediately. You do not need to restart the associated VPC vRouter.

3. IPv6 public networks do not support the SNAT service. For dual-stack public networks, the SNAT service takes effect on IPv4 addresses only.

4. If the associated VPC vRouter uses the OSPF protocol for communications, disable the SNAT service. This ensures effective communications for the VPC vRouter.
vpc.vrouter.attach.network.field.enableS:
### Enable SR-IOV
1. Make sure that the L3 network enables the SR-IOV feature. Otherwise, you could not enable the SR-IOV feature for the L3 network.
2. Make sure that the physical NICs connected to the L3 network have available VF NICs. Otherwise, you could not enable the SR-IOV feature for the L3 network.
3. By default, the switch SR-IOV is not selected, which means that the SR-IOV feature is disabled. In this case, you can attach vNIC-type NICs to VM instances.
4. If selected, the SR-IOV feature is enabled. In this case, you can attach VF-type NICs to VM instances.
vpc.vrouter.attach.publicNetwork.field.s:

3. If enabled, a VF NIC is attached to the VPC vRouter.
4. To enable SR-IOV, ensure the following points:
    - The VPC vRouter uses an openEuler system.
    - The L2 network of the public network uses SR-IOV network acceleration mode.
    - There are available VF NICs based on the physical NIC corresponding to this public network.

### Cluster Binding

1. If set to true, the vRouter\'s cross-cluster migrations are restricted. You can further define which migration operations are restricted through the cluster setting Resource Binding Policy.
2. If the cluster setting is Soft Binding:
    - The VPC vRouter starts only in the current cluster by default. If no available hosts exist in the current cluster, the VPC vRouter fails to start.
    - You can manually migrate the VPC vRouter to another cluster through the Change Host or Change Host and Primary Storage action.
3. If the cluster setting is Hard Binding: 
     - The VPC vRouter starts can only in the current cluster. If no available hosts exist in the current cluster, the VPC vRouter fails to start.
     - You cannot manually migrate the VPC vRouter to another cluster through the Change Host or Change Host and Primary Storage action.
4. If set to false, the VPC vRouter is not bound to the current cluster and can start in or be migrated to another cluster.
